But our full-cache sequential minimal optimisation (SMO) code ties or beats it on kernel $L_2$ margins, LIBLINEAR's dual solver is up to $4.5\times$ faster on the separable $L_2$ margin, and our solver is one to three orders of magnitude slower than LIBLINEAR's Newton solver on dense-support $L_2$ margins and than LIBSVM on a nearly touching kernel hull. Its edge is the certificate, not speed.

title: How Shared Representations Become Specialized: Formation, Maintenance, and Latent Susceptibility
subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Neural and Evolutionary Computing (cs.NE)
abstract: When several predictions use the same internal representation, information about some targets can remain easier to recover than information about others. We study how this specialization forms, persists, and changes in minimal artificial learners. With reconstruction errors weighted equally during learning, changing which target is observed precisely selects the favored target and redirects an already specialized learner. Removing current support can reduce a formed bias, whereas state-following update feedback can maintain it. We then compare learners formed through different observation and update conditions but matched on specified reconstruction measurements. Both change under the same brief opposing intervention, yet their responses differ. Resetting Adam largely removes the ten-update difference; exchanging its second moment reverses which route is more susceptible. New interventions show that equalizing the mean second-moment scaling reduces but does not remove the difference: its coordinate-wise pattern also matters. With fresh Adam or calibrated SGD, smaller route differences emerge later, whereas 500 common opposing updates bring the selected allocation endpoints close. A further control produces response differences with identical acquisition and equal mean loss weights but jointly different weight variability and realized sequence. Acquisition-selected formation also extends to a symmetric three-target setting. These interventions distinguish specialization's formation, present support, and time-dependent latent susceptibility.

title: LLM Value Functions for Credit Assignment in Agentic RL
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) for large language model (LLM) agents remains challenging in long-horizon tasks with sparse outcome rewards, where assigning credit to individual actions is difficult. Methods such as GRPO assign the same trajectory-level advantage to all actions, while critic-based methods require learning an additional value function that can be costly and unstable. We introduce LLM Value Function RL (LVRL), which uses the pretrained knowledge and in-context learning ability of an LLM to estimate policy-aware state values without finetuning a separate critic. LVRL conditions the value model on group context and calibrates its predictions using known values at the initial and terminal states, enabling step-level credit assignment from estimated value differences. We further extend this idea to learning from an expert policy through on-policy distillation (OPD), introducing LLM Value Function OPD (LVOPD), which focuses teacher supervision on actions associated with decreases in estimated value. We evaluate our approach across diverse agentic benchmarks: AppWorld, BabyAI, and SWE-bench Verified. Across policy scales (4B to 32B), LVRL consistently and substantially outperforms both GRPO and PPO. On AppWorld and SWE-bench Verified, LVRL yields absolute improvements of up to 13.6 and 8.6 percentage points over GRPO. Notably, on tasks requiring extended exploration like BabyAI, LVRL bridges the gap from total failure to 75.0% success. Furthermore, LVOPD yields consistent improvements over standard distillation baselines on AppWorld. Finally, Monte-Carlo analysis confirms that our frozen critic accurately identifies semantic pitfalls and recoveries, proving that LVRL extracts robust, policy-aware step-level credit from sparse terminal outcomes.

title: What Do Sparse Autoencoder Feature Discovery Scores Identify? From Activations to Interventions
subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Computation and Language (cs.CL); Machine Learning (stat.ML)
abstract: Sparse autoencoder (SAE) features are typically discovered from how their activations co-vary with behaviour, yet they are often used through interventions such as steering or ablation. We take intervention attribution, the first-order effect of a specified intervention on the model output, as our estimand. For a broad class of response functions, we show that observational feature-discovery evidence generally does not identify this attribution, and derive an exact gradient-based decomposition of the gap between linear-probe predictions and intervention attribution. Across four model-SAE pairs, median probe-to-attribution magnitude ratios range from tens to hundreds, while attributions closely track small-step steering. For single-latent ablations with nonzero effects, gradient predictions match the realized sign in 91-97% of cases, compared with 17-35% for probe-implied changes. Attribution-selected sets also produce larger absolute mean ablation effects on held-out prompts than sets selected by correlation, rank tests or probe coefficients. Together, these results establish intervention attribution as a principled, gradient-estimable target for selecting SAE features for intervention.

title: GuidanceNFT: NFT-Based Reward Fine-Tuning of Guided Diffusion Models
abstract: DiffusionNFT (NFT) fine-tunes diffusion models toward task-specific rewards, but optimizing these rewards does not guarantee fidelity to the full prompt. Although classifier-free guidance (CFG) strengthens prompt alignment, NFT is formulated as a CFG-free method, and applying CFG to the fine-tuned velocity field can reduce the optimized reward. This motivates optimizing rewards over the guided output distribution while seeking to retain its prompt alignment. However, applying standard NFT directly to guided samples can cause reward degradation or training collapse. We trace this failure to a mismatch between the reference velocity used in the NFT loss and the score of the guided sample distribution, which biases the improvement direction. We propose GuidanceNFT, which estimates the matching reference velocity through online flow matching on guided samples and uses it to correct both regression terms. With an exact reference, the corrected objective recovers NFT's intended update. In our experiments, the learned correction sustains reward improvement under both explicit and built-in guidance. On SD3.5-M, GuidanceNFT achieves higher optimized rewards than NFT with and without CFG across GenEval, text-rendering, and multi-reward objectives, together with better overall prompt alignment as measured by off-domain evaluation metrics. Experiments on models with built-in guidance, including Model Guidance and ELF, further demonstrate improved ImageNet generation, a better perplexity-entropy tradeoff on OpenWebText, and higher accuracy on GSM8K.

title: A Hybrid Gaussian Process-Extreme Gradient Boosting Machine Learning Framework for Robust Knockdown Factor Prediction and Reliability-Based Design of Thin Spherical Shell Caps
abstract: Elastic buckling remains a critical concern in the design of deep spherical shell caps, given that experiments reveal a significant reduction of critical loads from those predicted by linearized eigen-buckling analysis. This discrepancy has been attributed to initial geometric imperfections and is often reconciled through a dimensionless parameter, namely the knockdown factor (KDF). However, conventional KDFs (NASA SP-8007; Eurocode 3) are highly conservative, as they represent the lower bound of an extensive body of experimental data. This study aims to narrow the conservatism in the KDFs for spherical shell caps through machine learning (ML) regression models trained on experimental data on spherical shell buckling. A hybrid model is proposed by combining Gaussian Process Regression (GPR) with Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), and its improved performance is demonstrated over conventional ML algorithms, i.e., the Artificial Neural Network (ANN), Support Vector Regressor (SVR), Random Forest Regressor (RFR), and Histogram-based Gradient Boosting (HGBoost). Each of these models uses six input features and a single output, i.e., the KDF. The most critical feature affecting the KDF is ascertained through a sensitivity analysis. The study concludes with a reliability-based design framework that relies on the predictive ML model to obtain safety-consistent, yet less conservative, KDFs.

title: Make Every Expansion Count: Learning to Search Efficiently in LLM Code Repair
subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Software Engineering (cs.SE)
abstract: Large language model (LLM) code-repair systems fix faulty programs by repeatedly generating and testing revisions. Each revision is costly, making the choice of which repair to pursue important for efficiency. Existing search policies rely on test pass rates and search statistics, ignoring the details of test failures and proposed edits. We introduce CodeTriage, a learned policy that prioritizes edits before their revised programs are generated and tested. Its 0.6B-parameter model reads the test output, failure diagnosis, and proposed edit, then predicts a distribution over the number of repair steps needed to reach a fix through that edit. These predictions prioritize all pending edits across programs before generating and testing the revised code. On held-out repair tasks, CodeTriage finds fixes with 21% fewer program revisions and 12% fewer output tokens than the strongest baseline on each metric. Without retraining, it achieves the highest average success across search budgets for each of 11 unseen repair LLMs. Ablations show that both the failure context and edit text, as well as comparisons across programs, improve search. We also release a corpus of 12.2 million program versions from four LLMs, organized into repair trees with proposed edits and test results.

title: Sample-Optimal Multi-Group Learning with an ERM Oracle
subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Data Structures and Algorithms (cs.DS); Computer Science and Game Theory (cs.GT)
abstract: In multi-group learning, a single predictor must perform nearly as well as the best hypothesis in a class on every group in a rich, possibly infinite and overlapping, collection of subpopulations. The known algorithms with the optimal sample complexity keep track of every pair of a group and a hypothesis, which is impossible for the large classes of interest, and the known oracle-based algorithms have a worse rate. We ask whether the optimal rate can be attained by a learner that accesses the classes only through an empirical risk minimization (ERM) oracle. We give an algorithm that uses $\tilde{O}((d_G+d_H)/\varepsilon^2)$ samples and polynomially many calls to a weighted ERM oracle over pairs of a group and a hypothesis, where $d_G$ and $d_H$ are the VC dimensions of the group and hypothesis classes and $\varepsilon$ bounds the excess risk on every group, weighted by its probability. We also show a matching lower bound of $\Omega((d_G+d_H)/\varepsilon^2)$ samples for every learner even with unlimited computation, so oracle efficiency costs no additional samples. We also consider a natural special case in which every input belongs to at most $k$ groups and these groups can be listed. In this case, an ERM oracle for the hypothesis class alone suffices, with $\tilde{O}((d_H+\log k)/\varepsilon^2)$ samples in the agnostic setting and $\tilde{O}((d_H+\log k)/\varepsilon)$ samples when every group has a hypothesis that is correct on it.

title: Fast and Accurate: Improving Personalized LLM Performance by Semantic Concentration Inspired Workload Split between RAG and Fine-Tuning
abstract: With ever increasing personalized large language model (LLM) services, the next question to answer is how to improve the quality of services/users' experiences, which is indicated by personalized LLM generation accuracy/quality and inference latency. Although state-of-the-art designs, e.g., parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT), retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) or Full PEFT+RAG, can help, they largely ignore the heterogeneous semantic concentrations of users' historical data and cannot fully unleash the potential of personal data for personalized LLM performance enhancement. In this paper, we propose PEFT Union RAG (PUR), a novel ``fast and accurate'' approach that exploits the semantic concentration of users' personal historical data to split workload between PEFT and RAG, aiming to improve personalized LLM performance in terms of better generation accuracy/quality and lower inference latency. Briefly, PUR partitions user's personal historical data and assigns semantic concentrated ``core'' information to PEFT for offline parametric fine-tuning, while retaining dispersed information for RAG. During the online LLM inference, PUR directly generates responses for ``core'' queries covered by the PEFT region and invokes RAG only for sporadic ``peripheral'' queries. Experimental results show that, by appropriately splitting workload between PEFT and RAG, PUR consistently achieves the best generation accuracy/quality for various users across multiple tasks, while reducing inference latency by 14.4%--46.6% compared with the best performed method.

title: Mesh-Free Convolution: Learned Spectral Attenuation and Transport
abstract: Learning solution operators for partial differential equations (PDEs) requires models that can represent spatial structure across grids and scales. This becomes especially important in time-dependent problems, where the learned operator is often used autoregressively: each predicted state is fed back as input to predict future states. In this setting, small spatial errors can be repeatedly propagated through the learned dynamics, leading to instability and drift, vitiating long-term solution fidelity. We propose Mesh-Free Convolutions (MFCs), filters defined in continuous space and discretized only at evaluation time. This allows the same learned filters to be applied across resolutions. Rather than imposing a grid-dependent stencil or a fixed spectral cutoff, MFCs learn smooth scale-dependent filtering and include directional terms for transport-like behavior. Across fluid-dynamics and weather-forecasting benchmarks, MFC-based models produce stable long-horizon rollouts, transfer reliably across resolutions, and better preserve long-time statistics. These results suggest that continuous, mesh-free filtering is a useful inductive bias for PDE operator learning, especially in autoregressive prediction.

title: Error-Based Bidirectional Predictive Coding Enables Deep, 4-Bit Predictive Coding Networks
abstract: Predictive coding networks (PCNs) promise properties not offered by backpropagation-trained networks: learning from purely local information, a single network that both discriminates and generates, and flexible inference by energy minimization. However, their iterative inference is expensive, making hardware acceleration desirable, and a useful, efficient accelerator needs both depth and aggressive quantization. Canonical state-based PC delivers neither: its inference signal decays exponentially with depth, so deep models fail to train, and low precision makes it worse. We show that pairing two recent methods carries the full PCN property set into the deep, 4-bit regime: bidirectional PC (bPC), which unifies discrimination and generation, and the error-based reparameterization (ePC), which optimizes prediction errors rather than states during inference. Error optimization delivers the output signal to every layer in a single backward pass, removing the signal decay; one additional element, global-norm clipping of the error gradients, stabilizes the error dynamics at depth. The resulting ePC+bPC model trains stably up to at least eight layers and retains its full-precision accuracy and clean class-conditional generation under W4A4E4 quantization-aware training, across FP4 and three posit formats. On six-layer networks, where state-based bPC collapses to chance, ePC+bPC classifies more than 50 accuracy points above it after one epoch of training, with class-conditional generations 5-9x better in RMSE. 4-bit quantization is nearly free: full-precision and 4-bit accuracies differ by at most ~5 points, and by under two in the best-performing formats. We characterize the two failure modes the method overcomes, bounded signal decay in state-based PC and error divergence in unregularized error optimization, and discuss implications for a 4-bit-native PCN accelerator.

title: Instance-Adaptive Online Multiclass Multicalibration
abstract: We study online multiclass multicalibration over $T$ rounds, and give an algorithm with beyond-worst-case guarantees. With $n$ possible outcomes, forecasts lie in a simplex of dimension $d=n-1$. In the worst case, cumulative $\ell_1$ multicalibration error scales with $\widetilde\Theta(T^{(d+1)/(d+2)})$, which becomes untenable once $d$ exceeds a small constant. Our algorithm adapts to the geometry of the realized sequence: if the sequence of adversarially selected outcome means lies in an affine subspace of dimension $s$, it obtains error $\widetilde O(n^{1/(s+2)}T^{(s+1)/(s+2)})$ with high probability. The algorithm adapts to this structure without knowing the subspace or its dimension. For $T\ge n\ge2$, this rate is minimax optimal up to polylogarithmic factors. For a stochastic instance with a fixed conditional mean, the bound specializes to $\widetilde O(\sqrt{nT})$, giving a square-root dependence on the horizon.

title: Scaling Repeated-Data Pretraining: Batch Size, Regularization, and GPU-Time Tradeoffs
abstract: We study pretraining when compute is abundant but unique training data are finite, requiring repeated training on the same data. We first revisit infinite-compute pretraining (Kim et al. 2026) and show that its frontier depends critically on choices previously fixed or studied only in isolation. In particular, optimizing batch size together with epoch counts reveals a U-shaped relationship between validation loss and batch size, favoring smaller batches than typical pretraining, likely because small-batch gradient noise provides implicit regularization. We further find that training recipes, previously optimized under a single-pass assumption, can be tuned, e.g., repacking documents into new sequences every epoch, weight tying, and positive embedding weight decay. We then relax the infinite-compute assumption. In particular, smaller-than-typical batch sizes can require prohibitively long sequential training, motivating to treat GPUs and time as separate resources. Tighter deadlines favor larger batches, and latency-oriented parallelism can trade additional GPUs for shorter training. Nevertheless, even under a fixed time budget, a smaller batch with fewer GPUs can achieve lower validation loss than a larger batch with more GPUs, challenging the common practice of increasing data parallelism to maximize GPU utilization under a deadline. Together, our results identify underexplored factors in repeated-data training and provide concrete guidance on how training recipes and resource allocation should change from single-pass pretraining.

title: Softmax-Free Attention in Spiking Transformers as the Zero-Temperature Limit of Two-Level Systems
abstract: Spiking Transformers achieve energy efficiency by discarding softmax normalization in favor of thresholded, binary attention. However, this removal breaks the thermodynamic framework used to analyze attention networks, as the normalized measure and partition function cease to exist. We restore this theoretical foundation by proving that softmax-free spiking attention operates exactly as the zero-temperature limit of a product of independent two-level systems. This correspondence places spiking attention strictly in the frozen ordered phase of the thermodynamic phase diagram for all inputs. Consequently, the entropic cost of organizing attention collapses, replaced by a Landauer-type physical floor governed by action-potential generation. Furthermore, this ordered-phase pinning mathematically explains the optimization difficulty caused by vanishing surrogate gradients. We validate this theory with forward-relaxation experiments, placing both standard and neuromorphic attention mechanisms on a unified thermodynamic axis.

title: Probabilistic Forecasting of Wildfire Size Using Conditional Flow Matching
comments: 18 pages, 7 figures, 1 table. Code and data: this https URL
abstract: In this work we present a probabilistic model for predicting the temporal evolution of wildfire size using conditional generative algorithms, namely flow matching. Rather than predicting spatially resolved fire progression, the proposed model forecasts a time series of fire acreage, substantially reducing computational cost and enabling efficient integration with downstream applications such as early warning systems and risk assessment tools. Given estimates of the fire size at the current and previous forecasting steps, alongside spatially averaged weather conditions, terrain characteristics, and fuel composition, the model predicts the change in fire area over a 3-hour interval. Training data are drawn from 140 coupled atmosphere-wildfire simulations generated using WRF-SFIRE, paired with weather data from the North American Mesoscale (NAM) model. Sensitivity analysis demonstrates that the model captures physically-consistent responses to variations in wind speed, temperature, and relative humidity. Model performance is evaluated against reference solutions from WRF-SFIRE. For single-step predictions, the model achieves a symmetric mean absolute percentage error (sMAPE) of 0.39 relative to the reference WRF-SFIRE solutions. Recursive multi-step predictions over 24 hours are performed for 12 held-out test cases, where the flow matching model achieves a final fire area sMAPE of 0.39 while further providing meaningful quantification of forecast uncertainty.

title: Dissipative Lagrangian Neural Networks for the Interpretable Modelling of Passive Mechanical Systems
subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Computational Engineering, Finance, and Science (cs.CE)
abstract: In this paper, we propose the Dissipative Lagrangian Neural Network (dLNN), a continuous-time system identification technique that separately learns the conservative and dissipative dynamics of a mechanical system directly from data. A key contribution is a novel parametrisation of dissipative forces that (i) is structurally constrained to be dissipative, enforcing passivity of the learned model, (ii) cannot absorb conservative mechanics, and (iii) retains sufficient expressivity to represent a broad family of state-dependent damping and regularised friction forces. The model is validated on prediction tasks on two real-world mechanical systems: trajectory prediction of a chaotic double pendulum and inverse-dynamics modelling of a six-degree-of-freedom industrial robot. Across these tasks, the dLNN demonstrates improved predictive performance over existing Lagrangian architectures while remaining competitive with a black-box neural model. The imposed physical structure also improves generalisation to unseen states, with the benefits becoming particularly pronounced when training data is limited. Finally, we introduce a symbolic distillation procedure that extracts closed-form expressions from the learned physical components. Applied to the industrial robot, this produces interpretable symbolic models that retain high predictive accuracy while reducing the computational overhead associated with evaluating neural Lagrangian models.

title: A 4-Qubit Variational Quantum Classifier for Sequence-Specific Classification of DNMT3A and DNMT3B Flanking Methylation Preferences
comments: Accepted at IEEE International Conference on Quantum Artificial Intelligence (QAI) 2026
abstract: DNA methylation is a critical epigenetic modification that regulates gene expression and genome stability, primarily catalyzed by the DNA methyltransferase 3 (DNMT3) family of enzymes. Distinguishing precise sequence-specific flanking preferences between DNMT3A and DNMT3B remains computationally challenging due to the complex and high-dimensional nature of biochemical sequence data. In this study, we propose a novel Quantum Machine Learning (QML) approach to classify DNA methylation preferences, leveraging a Variational Quantum Classifier (VQC). Using experimentally derived deep enzymology data, we constructed a dataset containing 4,096 unique NNNCGNNN motifs. We evaluated a four-qubit VQC using a custom NumPy exact-statevector simulator. The described two-layer circuit contains 24 trainable rotations, eight CNOT gates, and eight input-encoding rotations, totaling 40 gates before measurement. Across five initialization seeds, the revised VQC evaluation achieved a ROC-AUC of 0.661 pm 0.009, where variability denotes sample standard deviation. The held-out test partition is approximately balanced, containing 200 DNMT3A-labeled motifs and 210 DNMT3B-labeled motifs. An always-DNMT3B predictor achieves 51.2% accuracy and a balanced accuracy of 0.500 on this test partition. This proof-of-concept establishes a foundation for utilizing near-term quantum architectures in complex epigenetic classification tasks, paving the way for hybrid quantum-classical pipelines in bioinformatics.

title: Certified Robustness via Sparse Second-Order Cone Relaxations
abstract: Certified robustness is critical for deploying neural networks in safety-sensitive settings, but computing exact certificates typically requires solving nonconvex optimization problems. Practical verifiers use convex relaxations: linear programming (LP) relaxations are scalable but often too conservative, whereas semidefinite programming (SDP) relaxations can be substantially tighter but are computationally expensive. We introduce a hierarchy of second-order cone programming (SOCP) relaxations that provide stronger certificates than LP while avoiding the cost of global positive-semidefinite constraints. Our construction combines convex-hull relaxations of ReLU activations, selective McCormick lifting over certified variable bounds, and second-order cone constraints induced by 2-by-2 principal minors. Adding these constraints progressively yields a monotone hierarchy of increasingly tight bounds with a controllable computation-tightness trade-off. On fully connected and convolutional networks on MNIST and CIFAR-10, SOCP-based verification improves certified robust accuracy over LP-based verification and is competitive with alpha,beta-CROWN, while remaining orders of magnitude faster than SDP-based verification. These results position selective second-order constraints as a practical middle ground between scalable LP-based and tight SDP-based certification. Finally, we introduce class-optimized robust evaluation (CORE), which applies tighter relaxations only to target classes not certified by cheaper ones. On the fully connected MNIST benchmark, CORE variants match SDP-cert's certified robust accuracy while reducing average verification time by up to 86.30%.

title: Autoregressive Decoding as a Martingale: Characterizing the Stochastic Dynamics of LLM Generation
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable success across a wide range of language tasks. At their core, autoregressive LLMs are conditional probability models that learn to approximate the next-token distribution given the preceding context. Despite this probabilistic nature, the stochastic dynamics of autoregressive decoding have rarely been investigated from a rigorous probabilistic perspective. In this work, we define the per-step prediction error as the difference between the sampled token indicator and the model's conditional predictive distribution, and prove that the cumulative error process is a martingale with respect to the decoding filtration, implying that its conditional first-order moment is identically zero. Beyond this first-order property, we derive a closed-form expression for the second-order behavior of the martingale sequence: its predictable quadratic variation reduces to $\sum_t\left(1-p(y_t\mid y_{<t})\right)$, computable from realized token probabilities alone. This identity establishes a direct theoretical connection between sequence fluctuations and predictive uncertainty during autoregressive decoding. White-box experiments on Llama-3.x and Qwen2.5 families (1B to 72B parameters) verify that the empirically measured second-order moments closely match the theoretical predictions derived from our martingale analysis. These results provide a probabilistic framework for analyzing autoregressive LLM decoding, reveal intrinsic probabilistic fingerprints of different language models, and establish a rigorous mathematical foundation for LLM-generated text detection and uncertainty quantification.

title: Backward Conformal Prediction under Covariate Shift
abstract: Backward conformal prediction (BCP) fixes the size of a prediction set and estimates its miscoverage, but assumes calibration and test data are exchangeable. We extend BCP to covariate shift through importance weighting, preserving its guarantees when the density ratio is known. We show that BCP's tight miscoverage report depends only on the relative weight assigned to missed calibration examples, explaining why a better domain classifier can sometimes produce a worse estimate. Motivated by the fact that BCP depends only on nonconformity scores, we propose estimating density ratios on sorted score vectors rather than high-dimensional inputs. We prove that this approach recovers the same report asymptotically under an interpretable condition and characterize the resulting bias otherwise. Experiments with simulated and benchmark distribution shifts show that the proposed method improves BCP's miscoverage estimates, while score-based weighting consistently yields more accurate estimates than embedding-based weighting.

title: Interpretable Graph Partitioning for Spatial Prediction
abstract: Spatial prediction estimates unobserved values from spatially distributed observations. Although flexible predictive models are increasingly available, their practical use remains limited when interpretability is essential. In this study, we formulate a graph partitioning problem to construct a global surrogate model that approximates black-box predictions with simpler representations. Specifically, we select connected subgraphs to minimize within-cluster residuals in vertex-level predictions. Although this formulation can be viewed as a variant of spatial regionalization, it operates on model-based predictions at individual locations rather than predefined areal units. With many locations, this point-level formulation may produce artificial connections between regions, reducing interpretability. We therefore introduce a constraint that excludes such connections while retaining flexible partition boundaries. We theoretically analyze how this constraint affects the resulting partition. We also develop a computational procedure for adjusting partition boundaries. Experimental results show that the proposed method yields spatially coherent partitions with flexible boundaries.

title: Memorization in image classification: test set behavior and scaling laws
comments: 11 Pages, 4 figures, Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Neural Network Artifacts as a New Data Modality
abstract: Deep neural networks are capable of both learning generalizing solutions on natural tasks and memorizing arbitrary mappings. We argue that understanding the former requires understanding the latter, which is much less studied. In what ways do networks that generalize or memorize differ in their behavior or their training dynamics? Do memorizing networks simply function as a lookup table where input-output mappings are stored independently? We investigate these questions in the context of CNNs trained on image classification tasks with randomized labels or pixels. We first study the behavior of such memorizing networks on unseen images. We find that independently initialized networks trained on the same random labels learn different predictive functions: they make different predictions on test examples, in contrast with generalizing networks. We then examine the effect of dataset size on memorization through the required network capacity and training time to interpolate the training set. Counter-intuitively, we find that the number of presentations of a given example required for complete memorization can decrease with dataset size even when input-output pairs share no common structure. Although memorizing networks do not learn a universal solution, they exhibit interesting behaviors which call for further investigations into the underlying mechanisms.

title: SelectTTRL: Representation-Guided Data Selection for Efficient Test-Time Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Test-Time Reinforcement Learning (TTRL) enables large language models to adapt directly on unlabeled test problems by constructing pseudo-labels from multiple sampled responses. However, existing TTRL methods typically apply the same expensive sampling and optimization procedure to all test problems, despite substantial differences in their training utility. In this paper, we study whether such problems can be identified before costly test-time training, without access to ground-truth answers. We uncover a stable relationship between internal response representations and problem-level empirical accuracy. Specifically, we define COS as the cosine similarity between a model's response representation and a correctness-related direction constructed from an independent question-answering dataset. COS consistently correlates with problem solvability across different models, datasets, and experimental settings, and we further provide a theoretical analysis explaining this relationship. Building on this finding, we propose SelectTTRL, a representation-guided data selection method that ranks test problems using COS and applies TTRL only to a selected percentile interval. SelectTTRL leaves the standard TTRL pipeline unchanged for the selected problems, while avoiding unnecessary multi-response sampling and reinforcement learning updates on the remaining ones. Experiments across multiple reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that SelectTTRL substantially reduces test-time computation while maintaining or improving the performance of standard TTRL. Code is available at this https URL.

title: Beyond Policy Rollouts: Embedding-Space Directional Exploration with Anchored Noise for LLM RLVR
abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) typically uses small rollout groups per prompt, where repeated sampling from the same policy can yield highly similar trajectories, reducing within-group reward variation and weakening group-relative advantage signals. Existing remedies such as higher sampling temperature, entropy bonuses, asymmetric clipping, and larger rollout budgets broaden sampling or modify policy updates but leave rollout conditioning unchanged. In this paper, we propose EDEN (Embedding-space Directional Exploration via anchored Noise), which intervenes at the rollout source through anchored input perturbations. EDEN explores beyond the policy's own rollouts. Within the same rollout budget, it replaces a small fraction of standard rollouts in each group with rollouts that the same policy generates from the prompt plus a single appended, perturbed embedding position, rather than from the prompt alone. Gaussian noise drives variation, while a shared anchor provides a common conditioning direction within each prompt group. Selected perturbed rollouts contribute to GRPO updates with downweighted advantages, and the model architecture, discrete decoding, and test-time inference remain unchanged. Across model scales and mathematical reasoning benchmarks, EDEN outperforms GRPO and the exploration controls evaluated in the same pipeline, with the largest gains in sampled solution coverage. Analyses show that more prompt groups provide non-zero group-relative learning signals and that noise and anchoring play complementary roles. Intervening at the rollout source is thus an effective lever for exploration in RLVR.

title: Silence and Noise: Resolving Suppression and Overvaluation in Multimodal Entity Alignment
comments: 26 pages, including appendices. Code: this https URL
abstract: Multimodal entity alignment (MMEA) is fundamental to integrating heterogeneous knowledge graphs (KGs), yet existing paradigms remain critically vulnerable to incomplete modalities and cross-graph structural asymmetries. This paper exposes a fundamental oversight in current MMEA research: treating feature missingness and topological discrepancies as isolated preprocessing or denoising challenges, which overlooks their destructive coupling during multimodal fusion. We systematically formulate and evaluate two newly identified failure modes: 1) Detail Missing (DM)-induced overvaluation, where the absence of local modality details causes models to overemphasize uninformative, blurred representations; and 2) Context Imbalance (CI)-induced suppression, where topological discrepancies across KGs allow dense structural contexts to overwhelm weaker but highly discriminative modal signals, triggering high-level semantic drift. To break this cycle of degradation, we introduce ALMEA, a generative and calibration framework that establishes a bidirectional feedback loop between low-level feature reconstruction and high-level latent space alignment. Specifically, Cross-Modality Imputation (CMI) synthesizes missing modality details to mitigate overvaluation, while Latent Semantic Calibration (LSC) aligns cross-graph joint embeddings to suppress topology-driven semantic drift. Under sparse supervision, we develop Controlled Iterative Selection (CIS) to adaptively acquire representative and diverse pseudo-labeled pairs, optimizing latent calibration under constrained budgets. Extensive evaluations on standard benchmarks demonstrate that ALMEA consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. At a 20% supervision rate, ALMEA yields substantial absolute improvements of up to 5.20% in MRR and 6.40% in Hits@1, maintaining robust gains across higher supervision thresholds.

title: XForecast: The KDD 2026 Finance Day Challenge on News-Grounded Financial Forecasting
abstract: Financial forecasting has traditionally relied on numerical time-series (TS) signals, while textual information such as news remains largely underutilized. We introduce XForecast, a benchmark and competition for news-grounded financial forecasting, where the task is to predict stock price movements four weeks ahead using both historical price data and paired news signals. XForecast combines stock price data with curated financial text generated using FinTexTS, a multimodal dataset generation method. It covers 100 large-cap stocks from 2019--2023, with training on 2019--2022 and evaluation on 2023. To better evaluate models that leverage textual signals, we adopt a weighted hit rate metric that places greater emphasis on instances where news information is expected to have stronger influence. The XForecast Challenge, hosted on Kaggle as part of KDD 2026 Finance Day, aims to benchmark methods for integrating financial TS and textual information.

title: BARTER: Compact Dynamic Sparse Training with Standard Dense Kernels
abstract: Dynamic sparse training (DST) aims to reduce training costs while maintaining accuracy. Existing DST methods mask out parameters but keep matrix dimensions unchanged. Training speedups therefore depend on specialized support, such as sparse kernels. We introduce BARTER, a structured DST framework that reduces training cost using standard dense kernels by keeping training tensors physically compact while dynamically reallocating capacity across layers. Unlike existing works that require computing gradients for all parameters, BARTER instead uses statistics collected only from active units during ordinary backpropagation to prune and clone attention heads and feed-forward channels under separate fixed global budgets. At each topology update, it resizes the affected parameter tensors and remaps their optimizer states, so subsequent training steps operate directly on the compact model. Training and fine-tuning experiments with Transformer-based vision models on two image classification benchmarks at densities from $0.1$ to $0.7$ show competitive Top-1 accuracy relative to full-tensor DST baselines. On an NVIDIA L40, BARTER achieves speedups of up to $6.29\times$ in measured training segments and reduces peak allocated GPU memory by up to $81.3\%$ relative to these implementations. An iPhone 13 Pro Max training benchmark additionally shows a $2.78\times$ speedup over the full-tensor DST baseline.

title: Fisher information and the geometry of memorization in neural networks
comments: 20 pages (10 pages main text), 11 figures (6 figures main text), NeurIPS 2026
subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Disordered Systems and Neural Networks (cond-mat.dis-nn); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)
abstract: A fruitful approach towards understanding generalization in machine learning involves characterizing how models separate generalizable structure from idiosyncratic or even corrupted features of training data. Fisher information has emerged as a diagnostic tool for this separation, leveraging loss geometry to distinguish generalization from memorization. Here we investigate this connection in vision models trained on CIFAR-10 with controlled noise that can be learned only through memorization. We show that projecting model weights onto the top Fisher eigenvectors decouples general task performance from noisy sample memorization, and we investigate how this decoupling presents differentially across layers. We show that the same phenomena are present in small transformers trained to solve a synthetic in-context learning task, and are reproduced in closed form in a simple, analytically solvable linear model. Our results reveal that Fisher information captures aspects of the geometric structure underlying how neural networks allocate capacity between generalization and memorization.

title: When Participant Disjoint Validation Is Not Enough to Establish Generalization in Parkinson's Gait Classification
comments: 9 pages, 5 figures. Includes supplementary analyses integrated into the appendices
abstract: Participant-disjoint cross-validation prevents direct participant overlap, but it may still produce optimistic estimates when acquisition site and diagnosis are structurally dependent. We examined Parkinson's disease classification using 159 pressure-walkway summary features from 133 WearGait-PD participants, including 65 participants with Parkinson's disease and 68 controls. The cohort was non-factorial: two sites contained only one diagnostic group, whereas VA-Seattle was the only site containing both groups. In repeated participant-level nested cross-validation, site alone achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.955 plus or minus 0.003, exceeding the gait-feature model (0.882 plus or minus 0.014). Under the evaluated logistic-regression pipelines, adding gait features to site, age, and sex produced no measurable improvement in pooled discrimination. More site-controlled evaluations produced lower and imprecise estimates: VA-Seattle same-site AUC was 0.668 (95% bootstrap confidence interval 0.477 to 0.836), and the JHOC + Bayview-to-VA-Seattle transport stress test achieved 0.576 (0.375 to 0.770). Supporting within-diagnosis site-prediction and site-conditioned permutation analyses showed that the gait representation retained substantial acquisition-site structure. These findings indicate that participant-disjoint pooled validation did not isolate disease-related discrimination from site-associated variation. They encourage careful examination of site-label dependence and, where possible, support for pooled results through within-site or independent validation before broader claims are made about generalization across institutions.

title: AutoNovo: Agentic Program Search Discovers Transferable Nucleic Acid Design Algorithms
comments: 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026). Workshop: Agentic AI for Biological Discovery
subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Quantitative Methods (q-bio.QM)
abstract: In-silico optimization of nucleic acids relies on predictive oracles that imperfectly capture biological function, so sequences optimized against one model may exploit model-specific artifacts and fail to generalize to independent models. Recent studies have shown that not all designers generalize equally well to independent models. In this work, we use agentic program search to iteratively propose, execute, evaluate, and revise code for nucleic-acid designers. We describe the successful strategies used to prompt the search. AutoNovo designers achieved the best observed mean among the evaluated methods on 3/3 DNA-design tasks in terms of in-silico performance, and 6/6 transfer tasks in terms of independent models. The designers come from a family of discovered nucleic acid designers rather than a single universal best designer. We plan to release the resulting designers. These results are the first steps in creating nucleic acid designers that maximize cross-model generalization, and thus improving the odds that in-silico designed sequences reflect real biology.

title: From Simulated Fluids to Living Tissue: Zero-Shot Foundation Model Transfer to Perturbed Embryos
subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Biological Physics (physics.bio-ph); Quantitative Methods (q-bio.QM)
abstract: Morphogenesis is driven by the interplay of genetic regulation and tissue mechanics. In vivo video data is limited, particularly under genetic mutations and environmental perturbations, making generalization beyond the most representative conditions in the dataset challenging. However, at tissue scales, the dynamics of Drosophila can be described as a continuum flow, motivating the usage of representations learned across other physical systems as priors for developmental dynamics. We investigate finetuning Walrus, a Continuum Dynamics Foundation Model pretrained across a broad set of simulated continuous systems, on tissue velocity fields from only 12 wild-type Drosophila blastoderm videos. We evaluate autoregressive prediction both in-distribution and zero-shot under unseen temperature and genetic perturbations. Zero-shot refers to evaluation on perturbation conditions never seen during wild-type finetuning, without any additional training. In-distribution, a Fourier Neural Operator model trained from scratch achieves best performance on VRMSE. However, Walrus (CRPS) is the strongest model under the most severe distribution shift of unseen samples of mutated embryos and temperature conditions. Interestingly, predictions capture the shape of the mean surface tissue velocity trajectory and its separation between 17°C and 27°C, including the timing of the peak at Germ Band Extension onset, a biologically meaningful milestone of embryo development. Our results provide preliminary support that representations learned from different dynamical systems can transfer to experimental morphogenesis in developmental regimes, provided they admit a continuum description. More broadly, our results motivate further study of physics foundation models as a new complementary tool for the simulation of morphogenesis in low-data regimes.

title: Spectral Considerations on Unsupervised Time-domain EEG Representation Learning with Deep Networks
abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) is a non-invasive, scalable source of quantitative biomarkers for the early diagnosis of brain disorders, and deep representation learning has become a powerful paradigm for extracting information-rich latent features from raw signals. However, neural networks tend to under-represent high-frequency information, a concern that is especially acute for EEG given its oscillatory nature and characteristic $1/f^\chi$ power decay, which risks masking disease-relevant high-frequency signatures. In this study, we systematically investigate the spectral constraints of unsupervised time-domain feature extraction across three autoencoder architectures (LSTMVAE, VAEEG, Transformer) and a state-of-the-art EEG foundation model. Using synthetic experiments and empirical validation, we show that while autoencoders capture macro-scale shifts such as alpha slowing, they remain biased against higher frequencies due to a magnitude-driven masking effect induced by the Mean Squared Error loss under 1/f-decaying spectra. Increasing latent dimensionality mitigates this attenuation but sacrifices latent compactness and generative stability. We argue that, as the field advances toward large-scale foundation-level feature extractors, it is imperative to move beyond simple time-domain reconstruction and to integrate spectral-domain loss terms and gradient-balancing techniques, so that the subtle high-frequency transients critical for diagnosing complex brain disorders are preserved in the latent representation.

title: Error Correction in Trained TTT Layers
comments: 13 pages, 3 figures. Code and saved results included as ancillary material and at this https URL
abstract: Test-time-training (TTT) layers update fast-weight memory while processing an input sequence. A gradient-based update, however, does not by itself establish how the memory revises an existing association. We study the structure and empirical role of prediction-derived updates in released TTT implementations. For dot-product objectives, we characterize the absence of a prediction-error residual and establish conditions under which inner-loop ascent and descent are equivalent after reparameterization. For the LayerNorm-based squared-error objective used by TTT-Linear and TTT-MLP, we derive the inner gradient and identify a prediction-derived component that cancels at the released initialization in the zero-epsilon limit. We then measure the full normalized prediction's contribution on three trained checkpoints. Removing this contribution while retaining the LayerNorm Jacobian gives a mean gradient norm ratio of 0.25 to 0.32 across the models. On 100,303 tokens from War and Peace, the same intervention with local per-token norm matching raises perplexity by 2.8-2.9% on TTT-Linear-760M and 1.3B, whereas freezing all fast-weight updates raises it by factors of 4.2-4.5. Separate synthetic tests illustrate the dependence of plain delta-rule overwriting on step size. The results distinguish a prediction-derived update from its behavioral value and show why implementation analysis and live interventions are both needed to assess test-time memory.

title: Fast Quantized Johnson$-$Lindenstrauss Transforms
subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Data Structures and Algorithms (cs.DS)
abstract: Quantization has emerged as one of the primary techniques for reducing the memory footprint of large language models during inference. A prominent example is Quantized Johnson$-$Lindenstrauss (QJL), which compresses KV caches using 1-bit asymmetric quantization while approximately preserving the inner products required by the attention mechanism. Recent theoretical and practical work aims at replacing the dense Gaussian projections used by the aforementioned transforms with more structured embeddings $-$ such as compositions of randomized Hadamard transforms $-$ while retaining the same embedding dimension. In this paper, we introduce two constructions based on a composition of randomized Hadamard transforms, albeit with a Gaussian rather than Rademacher diagonal in the second stage. The first adds Gaussian dithering to smooth the quantizer, while the second inserts a random permutation to regularize the covariance structure of the resulting Gaussian measurements. We prove embedding-dimension and running-time guarantees analogous to those of Fast JL in the non-quantized setting. The first construction achieves $m=O(\varepsilon^{-2}\log^2(d/\delta))$, while the second achieves $m=O(\varepsilon^{-2}\log(d/\delta))$ under a restriction on $m$. Both constructions can be applied in $O(d\log d)$ time.

title: BehaviorFormer: Discovering Behavioral Patterns via Clusterable Next-Token Prediction
comments: Accepted at IEEE Conference on Games 2026
subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Human-Computer Interaction (cs.HC)
abstract: Discovering behavioral patterns in open-ended games is challenging due to the lack of clear objectives or ground-truth annotations. In this work, we extend a next-token prediction Transformer with the deep clustering algorithm DCSS to learn meaningful representations with well-separated clusters. In a controlled Minecraft session with 26 players, the method discovers 23 distinct behavioral patterns that generalize across the studied players, further refining structures present in self-supervised representations into clearly separable clusters. We group the clusters into seven interpretable categories covering stationary, roaming, travel, mining, base work, logging, and farming behavior.

title: Probabilistic Simulation of Gas-Liquid Interfaces with Coupled Flow Matching on Spherical Harmonics
abstract: Bubbly flows involve strongly coupled bubble motion, deformation, and hydrodynamic interactions, making high-fidelity simulation computationally expensive. We propose a neural surrogate that jointly predicts bubble trajectories and interface deformation in a compact, shared representation, replacing costly mesh-resolved simulation with fast generative inference. Because two-phase flow dynamics is nonlinear and chaotic, we treat forecasting as a conditional generative problem rather than deterministic regression, predicting entire future windows in a single pass. We train and evaluate the surrogate on BubbleSH, a Front-Tracking dataset of rising deformable bubble swarms, assessing performance using trajectory, shape, and distributional metrics over kinematic, morphological, and interaction-based properties. The surrogate reproduces key flow statistics while running several orders of magnitude faster than the underlying DNS solver.

title: Rescuing Points Trapped Inside Incorrect Decision Regions: A target for Evaluating and Improving Forward-Forward Learning
abstract: Forward-Forward learning replaces end-to-end backpropagation with local, layer-wise training objectives. Its variants are evaluated primarily by classification accuracy, often measured with linear probes trained on their representations. We show that this evaluation can over-credit the learning method: a linear probe on the representations of an untrained convolutional neural network already reaches accuracy well above chance. Moreover, a single accuracy value does not reveal which datapoints become correctly classified after training and which remain misclassified. To examine what learning contributes beyond the random, untrained baseline, we present an analysis methodology built on the Boundary Proximity Index (BPI), a multiclass margin normalized by a class-centroid reference. We apply our analysis to seven Forward-Forward variants and related layer-local methods and find that initially misclassified points near the probe's decision boundary generally have higher rescue rates than those farther inside incorrect decision regions. Rescue rates vary substantially across methods, with some correcting a substantial fraction of these deeply embedded points. Together, these analyses offer a way to evaluate representation learning beyond accuracy and identify the rescue of points far inside incorrect decision regions as a target for improving local learning methods.

title: A Production-Grade, High-Efficiency Agentic RL Framework for Frontier LLMs with Validated Recipes
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a critical phase in the post-training pipeline of large language models (LLMs). As the frontier of LLM capabilities shifts from static reasoning to agentic tasks--characterized by external tool invocation, multi-turn interactions, and long-horizon decision-making--existing mainstream RL frameworks have grown increasingly unwieldy, raising the overhead of adoption, usage, and debugging. To address these challenges, we present LoongSage, an agent-native, fully asynchronous RL framework with a lightweight core of roughly 14K lines of code. Built upon Megatron for distributed training and SGLang for high-throughput inference, LoongSage centralizes orchestration within a single controller process and encapsulates all GPU-resident components as Ray actors. It introduces AgentFlow, a unified execution paradigm that orchestrates both white-box and black-box agents. For asynchronous execution, it integrates sliding-window strategies that bound trajectory staleness, and employs TransferMesh, a topology-aware synchronization mechanism that routes weights after each step over the fastest transport available to each receiver. Beyond agentic RL, LoongSage incorporates a memory-efficient Teacher Manager that decouples the scaling of teacher models from GPU memory constraints, natively supporting Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation. Extensive evaluations across four complete training runs, spanning complex reinforcement learning and multi-teacher distillation, demonstrate that task rewards improve steadily while the train-inference gap is kept under continuous control, and the fully asynchronous pipeline removes synchronous idle bubbles, sustaining hardware utilization.

title: Sampling from Neural Operator Priors to Solve Partial Differential Equations
abstract: Guided sampling with sparse observations and PDE residuals has recently been combined with neural operator priors to solve partial differential equations in function space, their natural setting. We pair such a prior with pseudo-bootstrap sequential Monte Carlo (pBS SMC), a guided sampling framework that accommodates proposals without tractable densities, and introduce a new proposal by adapting the DPM++ algorithm to the guidance setting. Across five benchmark PDE systems this proposal attains the best error--time trade-off at every step count tested, and wrapping it in pBS gives the lowest error on most inverse-problem settings, with the largest gains when few sampling steps are used.

title: Resample the Answer: Where to Spend Test-Time Compute in Recursive Reasoning
abstract: Recursive reasoning models such as the Tiny Recursive Model (TRM) iteratively refine two latent states: an answer state y, decoded into the output, and a reasoning state z, which is never decoded. Many of their failures have been attributed to bad basins, regions of latent space that trap the recursion on wrong answers. Recent test-time approaches perturb y, z or both to recover these failures, but the impact of this choice on performance, test-time compute efficiency and scaling properties remains unclear. Through controlled experiments on TRM, we find that a failed trajectory carries its failure in its answer state. At equal compute, in depth and in width, resampling y recovers more failures than any perturbation of z we tested, and the performance gap widens as the test-time compute budget grows. Our approach, Gated Answer Resampling (GAR), pairs this resampling of the answer state with the model's own halting head and restarts only the puzzles that the head rejects. With at most 64 restarts per puzzle and no training or hyperparameter search, GAR takes TRM from 85.9% to 99.4% on Sudoku-Extreme and from 68.8% to 85.6% on Pencil Puzzle Bench validation. On the same checkpoints, GAR also outperforms Probabilistic TRM (PTRM), which perturbs z at each step, even when PTRM uses 42 to 197 times as much compute.

title: ECHO: Correcting Time Series Foundation Model Forecasts with Historical Analogues and Errors
abstract: Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) provide general-purpose forecasting capabilities, yet their forecasts can remain misaligned with the temporal characteristics of a target domain. This motivates lightweight forecast correction even when only black-box access to the TSFM is available. Our key observation is that two forms of historical information provide complementary correction signals: historical analogues reveal how similar contexts evolved, while past forecast errors reveal a TSFM's characteristic deviations in the target domain. Based on this observation, we propose ECHO, a black-box forecast correction framework that learns from both sources. ECHO uses AnalogE to assess retrieved historical analogues together with the current context and base forecast, learning transferable corrections through cross-domain pretraining. In parallel, RecentE learns target-specific residual corrections from past forecast errors and refines them as causally available feedback accumulates. ECHO dynamically combines the two corrections according to their observed forecasting performance. Across 5 representative TSFMs and 9 real-world datasets, ECHO reduces MSE in all 45 backbone--dataset settings, yielding an average relative reduction of 9.26\% in macro-average MSE. Its gains also extend to long-horizon forecasting.

title: StructZO: Structured Zeroth-Order Optimization for Memory-Efficient LLM Fine-Tuning
abstract: Fine-tuning large language models at scale is increasingly limited by the memory cost of backpropagation. Zeroth-Order (ZO) optimizers reduce this burden by relying only on forward function evaluations, but they still exhibit a substantial performance gap to first-order (FO) optimizers such as Adam. We argue that this gap does not arise solely from the absence of explicit gradients: FO fine-tuning also benefits from informative low-rank optimization geometry, large-scale signal aggregation, and well-conditioned update directions. Motivated by this, we introduce StructZO, a structured Zeroth-Order optimization framework for memory-efficient LLM fine-tuning. StructZO performs large-query ZO estimation within an activation-induced informative subspace and applies spectral control to the resulting reduced-space update before mapping it back to the original parameters. This lets ZO aggregate useful directional signals in a compact, geometry-aware space while avoiding the activation and optimizer-state memory costs of backpropagation. We show theoretically that, when the induced subspace captures concentrated optimization-relevant directions, StructZO reduces the effective ZO estimation dimension from $mn$ to $mr$, with the remaining projection error governed by the spectral tail of the activation Gram matrix. Empirically, across OPT-series and Llama3.1-8B on diverse downstreamtasks, StructZO improves over the strongest existing ZO baselines by up to $8.7%$ relative on average and up to $26.9%$ relative on individual tasks, while remaining within $1.5%$ of FO-Adam on average. These results suggest that structured and spectrally controlled ZO updates can substantially narrow the gap between ZO and FO optimization.

title: Growing and Transferring Pathways for LLM Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) can substantially improve the reasoning capabilities of large language models, but an effective training run requires considerable resources. Reusing the computation acquired through RL across models would extend the value of that training. We propose GrowRL, an RL method that organizes learned updates into compact computational pathways through structural growth. GrowRL freezes the pretrained backbone and adds an independent causal attention branch and a feed-forward network branch at each Transformer layer. Zero-initialized output projections preserve the pretrained policy at initialization, and RL updates only the added pathways. The learned pathways remain explicit after training, allowing transfer to structurally compatible target models and subsequent adaptation with the target backbone frozen. The architecture also supports sequential transfer of additional pathways. By keeping the learned attention and feed-forward computation separate from the pretrained weights, GrowRL provides an explicit structure for preserving and reusing the outcome of an RL run. Experiments across five backbones show competitive mathematical reasoning and out-of-distribution performance with a small number of trainable parameters. Learned pathways provide immediate gains across all three transfer directions, with performance after only 10 target-side updates already close to that after 100 updates in every case. These results support computational pathways as parameter-efficient and reusable units of reinforcement learning adaptation.

title: pi-Net: Empirical Latent Representations for Differentiable Physics Heads in Data-Scarce Systems
abstract: Developing reliable predictive models for multi-physics systems often forces a compromise between computationally demanding physical simulators and data-hungry, opaque machine learning (ML) algorithms. While incorporating dimensional analysis into directed computation graphs offers a structurally sound alternative to explicitly solving partial differential equations (PDEs), such formulations typically yield underdetermined systems that act as imperfect simulators. We introduce pi-Net, a physics-informed latent variable model that resolves these imperfect simulators. The hybrid pi-Net architecture consists of an encoder that maps inputs into physically normalized latent space, which are then decoded into final predictions by a differentiable physics head. Evaluated on a real-world, data-scarce Gas Metal Arc Welding (GMAW) case study, the framework achieves an R2 of 0.864 with only 60 experimental samples. The results demonstrate that pi-Net significantly outperforms purely data-driven baselines in data-scarce regimes while providing causal, process-level explainability.

title: Asymptotic Risk of Learning-Rate Schedules for Least-Squares Regression with Discretely Distributed Features
subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Optimization and Control (math.OC); Machine Learning (stat.ML)
abstract: We study the last iterate of stochastic gradient descent (SGD) on streaming least squares with discretely distributed features (Slock's model), which decouples the dynamics across eigendirections. Under power-law source and capacity conditions, we derive the exact finite-time risk and asymptotic equivalents of constant and Warmup-Stable-Decay (WSD) schedules. With a tuned base learning-rate, the resulting scaling law decays as $\Theta(T^{-q})$, where $T$ is the horizon, and $q$ is independent of the cooldown length $c \in (0,1]$ but is strictly smaller for the constant schedule: any cooldown of fixed relative length $c > 0$, however short, improves the risk by a polynomial factor, while its length only affects the constant, which is minimized by linear decay ($c = 1$). Finally, we show that the optimal risk depends on the batch size $b$ and horizon $T$ only through $bT$, up to a critical batch size.

title: Reinforcement Learning with Hawkes-Structured Networks for Market Making
abstract: Market making under realistic order-flow dynamics is challenging due to the clustered, self-exciting nature of order arrivals, which are naturally modeled by non-Markovian Hawkes processes. We propose a model-free reinforcement learning (RL) framework for market making with general Hawkes order-flow dynamics. We first establish non-asymptotic performance bounds that quantify the loss incurred by approximating the infinite-dimensional Hawkes state using a finite collection of exponentially weighted features. Guided by this analysis, we introduce the Hawkes-Structured Network (HSN), a novel neural architecture that encodes historical order flow through a learnable mixture-of-exponentials filter. HSN is trained end-to-end using model-free RL, jointly optimizing the feature representation and quoting policy directly from reward feedback. Experiments on single- and multi-asset market-making problems with mixture-of-exponentials, power-law, and regime-switching kernels demonstrate that HSN outperforms general-purpose neural architectures, achieving higher trading rewards while implicitly recovering the underlying order-flow intensities.

title: Learning Graded Sparse Mechanisms: A Representation Theorem and Certified Generalization
subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Multiagent Systems (cs.MA); Machine Learning (stat.ML)
abstract: In a variety of multi-agent and physical environments, an element's update depends strongly on a few other elements and weakly on many, and both the identity and the number of the elements that matter change with the state of the system. Such graded sparse mechanisms are common, for instance, in flocks, crowds, learned particle simulators and the neighborhood aggregation of graph networks, yet they have received little systematic study as a class of functions with the grading given. In this paper we study the supervised learning of the mechanism when the grading is provided by the environment, as a weight on every element. First, we define the class by axioms, where each element's influence is capped by its weight, the dependence on the weights is regular, and no element is distinguished, and prove a representation theorem: the class is exactly the Lipschitz ball of a transport metric on weighted multisets, and the metric is forced by the axioms. Next, the geometry of the representation gives generalization bounds that depend on the data in two ways. One is via the sparsity profile of the data -- the law of how many elements matter and by how much -- which bounds the rate over all designs with that profile, with an exponent from the profile and no dependence on the number of elements. In a number of natural cases we also show matching lower bounds, up to constants in the exponent. The other is empirical: due to the representation result, classical empirical discrepancy bounds apply to the class as they stand, and the resulting bound is the transport distance between the two halves of the sample in the class's own metric, computed exactly by a matching, with an additional concentration term. Finally, we study a simulated Vicsek flock under four interaction rules at two noise levels, and show that the certificate is non-vacuous, a small fraction of the trivial value on every rule.

title: DeepFlow: Two Convergent Differentiable Approaches for Pairwise Conditional Random Fields
abstract: Basic probabilistic models form the basis of modern deep learning largely by defining the final activation layer of a network and allowing the networks outputs to be interpreted through a probabilistic lens. By increasing the complexity of these final activation layers to include features such as spatial regularisation, allow for these models to improve in performance without requiring significantly more data. The challenge however is to ensure that these more complex probabilistic graphical models adapt well to being used in tandem with deep learning, that is, ensuring they converge and have meaningful derivatives. The goal of this paper is to show two algorithms with provable convergence properties to allow this type of regularisation for image and signal classification models. Through both rigorous mathematical analysis and in silico experiments, we can show the differing performance between these solution types.

title: Optimal Transport PAC-Bayes Bounds
abstract: PAC-Bayesian generalization bounds are among the strongest distribution-dependent guarantees in statistical learning and are typically expressed in terms of the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence between a prior and posterior distribution. While analytically convenient, the KL divergence requires the posterior to be absolutely continuous w.r.t. the prior, imposing support constraints that can substantially restrict the choice of posterior. Moreover, the KL divergence does not account for the underlying geometry of the probability space. In this work, we derive new PAC-Bayesian bounds replacing the KL divergence with general optimal transport (OT) distances, including the total variation and Wasserstein-$p$ distances.

title: The Language of Looking: Motion Tokens Reveal Domain-Dependent Local Structure in Gaze Sequences
abstract: Human gaze is the primary high-bandwidth interface through which we parse the semantics of our environment. While often modeled as a sequence, the degree to which gaze exhibits transferable local structure across domains remains underexplored. Using motion tokenization as a diagnostic lens across four diverse datasets, we investigate the transferability of local sequence structure. We demonstrate that while gaze can share a reusable motion-token vocabulary, identical motion tokens are organized into different local transition patterns depending on the dataset and task context. Our results show the limitations of naive data-pooling under low-semantic motion-token representations and provide a framework for evaluating behavioral sequences through information-theoretic diagnostics.

title: Characterizing and Mitigating Distributional Bias in Physics-Informed Generative Models
abstract: Physics-informed generative models augment a data-fitting objective with residual penalties that encourage physical constraints to hold in generated samples. However, improving constraint satisfaction need not improve fidelity to the data distribution. We study this conflict in residual-regularized diffusion models and identify two possible consequences. First, the same prediction error can incur different residual costs near different feasible states, preferring states with lower residual sensitivity (avoidance). Second, this preference can extend to feasible states outside the data support, where the residual also vanishes (leakage). Motivated by this analysis, we propose a data-anchored penalty that weights prediction errors by the residual Jacobian at the clean training sample and normalizes the resulting magnitude. This removes the incentive to relocate to less sensitive states without changing the model architecture or sampling procedure. Experiments on a controlled synthetic system, three PDE systems, and molecular transition-state generation with flow matching demonstrate the benefits of anchoring. Code is available at this https URL.

title: OctMole: Multiscale 3D Molecular Generation with Hierarchical Spatial Flows
abstract: Generating accurate 3D molecules requires jointly determining a variable number of atoms, their identities, and geometry across spatial scales: global shape emerges coarsely, whereas chemical bonds demand fine local precision. Existing atom-based diffusion and flow models operate largely at a single scale, while dense spatial fields become costly at high resolution. We introduce OctMole, a multiscale octree flow framework for 3D molecular generation. A hierarchical occupancy flow progressively resolves sparse molecular support from coarse to fine, and a joint atom flow assigns atom types and continuous in-cell offsets to occupied leaves. This decomposition combines efficient global structure with subcell geometric precision, while cell corruption improves robustness to generated support. On QM9 and GEOM-DRUG, OctMole achieves strong chemical, distributional, and geometric quality, with particularly clear gains over Uni-3DAR on GEOM-DRUG and substantial efficiency gains over dense 3D generation. As an additional capability, intermediate occupancy states and selected regions provide spatial conditioning without task-specific retraining, supporting multiscale shape conditioning, regional editing, linker generation, and shape interpolation. Code and pretrained checkpoints are available at this https URL and this https URL, respectively.

title: HyBRA-EEG: Hyperbolic Global-Local Brain-Region Aggregation for Self-Supervised EEG Representation Learning
abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) representation learning is challenged by noisy signals, inter-subject variability, and heterogeneous electrode montages in different datasets and recording settings. Recent self-supervised EEG pretraining methods improve transferability by converting heterogeneous recordings into unified token or sequence representations, but channel-aware designs may still encode montage- or dataset-specific regularities. We propose HyBRA, a self-supervised framework based on hyperbolic global-local brain-region aggregation. HyBRA maps heterogeneous channel observations into a fixed regional token space by combining electrode coordinates, region priors, and feature-dependent hyperbolic distances. A channel-evidence injection branch preserves fine-grained discriminative cues during aggregation. The resulting tokens are processed by a Region-Time Transformer and pretrained with masked reconstruction of latent features and region-level signals. HyBRA outperforms the compared methods in average balanced accuracy on six benchmark datasets. Under a controlled six-fold evaluation on OpenBMI-MI, HyBRA matches CSBrain in balanced accuracy, improves AUROC by 1.84 percentage points and AUPRC by 5.23 percentage points, and uses 96.8\% fewer parameters. Matched comparisons on TUAB and TUEV show higher balanced accuracy for hyperbolic matching than for Euclidean distance or cosine similarity.

title: DEFlow: Deep Equilibrium Flow Maximum-Entropy Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Expressive flow policies can represent multiple high-value actions, but sampling them with few integration steps while retaining tractable action densities remains challenging. We introduce DEFlow, a deep equilibrium flow policy that replaces explicit Euler sampling with implicit Euler integration and solves all intermediate actions jointly as an equilibrium system. We combine implicit differentiation with a discrete change-of-variables formula for the final-action density, enabling off-policy training within soft actor-critic without backpropagating through solver iterations. DEFlow achieves an average relative improvement of approximately 10% in mean successful coverage over the strongest baseline across four Multi-Goal docking variants. It also achieves the highest mean time-averaged return on four of five manipulation tasks, while remaining broadly competitive across five MuJoCo tasks. These results support implicit flow policies for tasks requiring both diversity and precision, at the cost of additional nonlinear and linear solves. Primary

title: DR-APO: Decoupled-Representation Advantage-Guided Policy Optimization from Continuous Control to Embodied Navigation
abstract: Policy representations in reinforcement learning have expanded beyond Gaussian policies to diffusion and flow-matching based generative policies. However, existing RL methods remain representation-specific, lacking a unified optimization interface for emerging generative policies. In particular, extending likelihood-based objectives to multi-step generative policies couples optimization to their internal generation process, where accumulated likelihood ratios can weaken the update signal.
