On two high-resolution 3D particle-accelerator benchmarks, bunched-beam transport and plasma-wakefield acceleration, GLOBE lowers relative-$L_2$ error by 9\% and 13\%, low-frequency spectral error by 69\% and 51\%, and mid-frequency spectral error by 54\% and 20\% relative to the strongest baseline (DPOT), satisfies field constraints, and reduces hours of PIC simulation to a minute per rollout.

title: Chunk-wise Model-based Policy Optimization
abstract: Model-based reinforcement learning has shown superior sample efficiency by leveraging the learned latent dynamics either in the form of derivative-free planning/imagined rollout training or dynamics gradient-based policy updates. While these approaches achieve comparatively fast learning, they all suffer, to varying degrees, from issues of recurrent compounding errors, high inference-time latency, and instability in backward propagation through time (BPTT). In this work, we propose a model-based RL approach that uses the chunk world model as a differentiable training-time evaluator to optimize the chunk actor without recurrent model invocation. Through the collaborative chunk-wise prediction of the world model and policy, we can generate H-step hypothetical rollouts in a single forward pass and directly optimize value expansion, avoiding the costly and unstable BPTT. We evaluate our method on 19 challenging high-dimensional humanoid tasks from HumanoidBench and deploy our method to the real-world for quadruped bipedal walking. Project Website: this https URL

title: Strong Gaussian Approximation of Constant-Learning-Rate SGD: Bias and Trajectory Inference
abstract: This paper develops strong Gaussian approximations (KMT type) for constant learning rate stochastic gradient descent (SGD). We work with heavy tailed noise and assume that the number of iterates grows and the learning rate shrinks simultaneously. Our work constructs simple Gaussian processes on the same space and bounds, in probability, the maximum difference between the SGD errors and their respective limits. While there exist central limit theorems for constant rate SGD centered at the optimum, these only provide individual iterate inference. By contrast, our quenched KMT approximations allow for finite sample, simultaneous, whole-trajectory-level inference and imply stochastic process convergence (Functional Central Limit Theorems (FCLTs)). For accumulated errors centered at the true optimum, we first obtain a KMT-type approximation bound when the learning rate scales as $\gamma_n=\frac{c}{\sqrt n}+o(n^{-1/2})$ for a constant $c \in \mathbb{R}^+$ and $n$ iterations. The result reveals a trade off between controlling the bias of SGD and the initialization effect, with no learning rate scaling generally making both contributions vanish in the accumulated error limit. To eliminate these contributions, we consider a Burn in scheme and Richardson-Romberg extrapolation and prove respective KMT and FCLT theorems. We also prove a finite-horizon KMT-type approximation and FCLT for the rescaled iterate trajectory to a stationary Ornstein--Uhlenbeck (OU) process. We consider applications in risk control and simultaneous inference and perform simulations to illustrate our results.

title: Dissecting the Carbon-SLO Tension in Geo-Distributed LLM Serving
comments: 13 pages, 8 figures. Code: this https URL
subjects: Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Performance (cs.PF)
abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) inference is driving a growing share of datacenter carbon emissions. Although carbon-aware scheduling can reduce these emissions in geo-distributed datacenters by exploiting the spatiotemporal variations in grid carbon intensity, the latency-sensitive nature of LLM serving constrains this design space. While prior studies investigate the carbon savings achievable through spatial scheduling, they oversimplify the dynamics of modern inference engines, such as queueing and continuous batching, which strongly shape inference latency. We address this issue by designing and evaluating a latency-centric, geo-distributed inference simulator, calibrated with hardware-grounded latency and power measurements, that reproduces these dynamics and enables the study of carbon savings under strict service-level objectives (SLOs). We then formulate a series of SLO- and carbon-aware schedulers of increasing sophistication, from per-request heuristics to batch-level optimization: (i) a greedy heuristic, (ii) an integer linear programming (ILP)-based scheduler jointly assigning batches of requests, (iii) an iterative ILP-based solution projecting its own assignments back into the load estimates to capture load coupling, and (iv) a facility mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) scheduler pricing the energy of batched requests collectively rather than in isolation. Across three LLMs under MLPerf SLOs and varying system loads, the MILP-based option offers the best carbon-SLO balance, reducing carbon emissions by up to 60% relative to the round-robin policy, with an average SLO violation of 3%. Our characterization further shows that savings grow with the spread of carbon intensity across datacenters and shrink as system load increases, while SLO attainment depends on how frequently schedulers receive datacenters' load updates.

title: Fine-Tuning Strategy, Not Just Data: A Statistically Rigorous Audit of Gender and Stereotypical Bias in Embedding Models for HR Recommendation Systems
comments: 8 pages, 4 figures, 5 tables. Accepted at RecSys in HR '26 (The 6th Workshop on Recommender Systems for Human Resources)
subjects: Information Retrieval (cs.IR); Computation and Language (cs.CL); Computers and Society (cs.CY); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
abstract: Embedding models underpin modern job-candidate matching: resumes, job descriptions, and queries are encoded as dense vectors, and recommendations come from nearest-neighbor retrieval over that space. Any social bias in the embeddings therefore feeds directly into HR recommendations. We audit six multilingual sentence-embedding models (LaBSE- and E5-family, both public and custom fine-tuned) using Bias-in-Bios (occupational gender bias) and StereoSet (stereotypes across profession, race, gender, and religion). We treat statistical validity as a first-class concern: we identify a non-independence error in a naive significance test, where pooling non-independent pairwise similarities inflated a trivial 0.0046 mean difference to $p \approx 0$, and replace it with a profession-level paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test, individual-resampling bootstrap confidence intervals, and permutation tests for StereoSet. Under the corrected methodology, knowledge-distillation (KD) fine-tuning of E5-Base significantly increases measured bias on Bias-in-Bios ($\Delta = -0.177$, $p < 10^{-8}$; more negative means more bias), although this measure is sensitive to global embedding geometry. The KD result is corroborated by pro-stereotype patterns in the StereoSet profession category (uncorrected $p < 0.05$). Binary-classification fine-tuning of the same base model shows no statistically distinguishable change ($p = 0.218$). Fine-tuning strategy is thus an actionable design lever for practitioners building HR recommenders. We also report which benchmark categories are underpowered, and note that two domain-adapted models could not be included in significance testing due to a software-access constraint, which limits our conclusions.

title: EarthAlign: Learning Language-Aligned Representations of Earth System Data
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
abstract: Interpreting Earth system conditions is central to understanding environmental risks and informing decisions across weather- and climate-sensitive sectors. Existing multimodal weather systems primarily target task-specific prediction, generation, or question answering, while general-purpose alignment between Earth system data and language remains underexplored due to the limited availability of diverse language supervision grounded in meteorological conditions. To fill this gap, we introduce EarthAlign, a large-scale dataset with broad geographic coverage spanning 2000-2024 that combines 10 expert-curated natural event and disaster data sources with climatology-derived normal-weather samples. Each sample includes temporal and geospatial information and four grounded caption styles aligned with 63-variable ERA5 meteorological data. Building on EarthAlign, we introduce MeteoLIP, a dual-encoder framework for learning aligned meteorology-language representations. MeteoLIP incorporates MetTok, which uses a geolocation- and time-conditioned query to aggregate variable-specific patch embeddings into a compact sequence of meteorology tokens. To comprehensively assess Earth system multimodal representations, we introduce three downstream tasks: cross-modal retrieval, weather-condition classification, and physical variable estimation. Our experiments show that MeteoLIP improves upon the corresponding CLIP and SigLIP baselines across these tasks. Further analyses highlight the importance of meteorological input, temporal and geospatial conditioning, and multi-style supervision for meteorology-language alignment. Thus, EarthAlign and MeteoLIP provide a foundation for learning and evaluating language-aligned representations of Earth system data. Our code, dataset, and weights are publicly available at this https URL.

title: Self-improving data synthesis can scale embedding models across domains and tasks
comments: 30 pages, 6 figures; supplementary information included (27 pages). Code: this https URL Data: this https URL
subjects: Information Retrieval (cs.IR); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
abstract: Adapting embedding models to new tasks requires training data that reflect task-specific information needs and relevance criteria. However, manual data design is costly and difficult to scale. Here we introduce SYNTRA, a novel retrieval data synthesis method whose self-improvement loop iteratively refines reusable synthesis instructions using feedback on trial outputs. This process requires only an unlabelled corpus and a few relevant query-document pairs. Experiments across 24 retrieval datasets spanning 15 domains demonstrate the effectiveness of the synthesized data. These data also improve widely used, strong embedding models on tasks with and without existing labelled training sets. Self-improvement enhances retrieval on all six evaluated tasks, outperforming human calibration on four. Moreover, retrieval performance continues to improve on MS MARCO as we scale the training dataset to 32 times its initial size. Overall, with minimal human intervention, SYNTRA enables scalable adaptation of embedding models across domains and tasks.

title: Rethinking Opinion Measurement Interfaces for Human-in-the-Loop Optimization
comments: 29 pages. Written in 2022, published as last revised. Dataset, analysis scripts, and system source code: this https URL
abstract: Human-in-the-loop optimization refers to systems that present choices to a human decision-maker and query their judgment to optimize system parameters iteratively. The user interface typically provides either an absolute rating scale or asks for a preferred option. However, these approaches can potentially suffer from calibration problems, inconsistencies, and completeness violations of user preferences in such a sequential evaluation. This paper revisits the design space of opinion measurement interfaces for human-in-the-loop optimization. We conducted a study (N=360) using text summarization and image color enhancement tasks to evaluate human sequential feedback in six representative opinion measurement interfaces. Based on our analysis, we recommend using a listwise approach to support sequential opinion measurement, which counterweighs individual rating and preferential choice limitations and conveys more information for subsequent use. We further discuss the trade-offs in different user interface designs and provide guidelines to inform future research.

title: KedgeFlow: A Programmable Control Plane for Enterprise AI Agents
comments: 12 pages, 1 figure, 3 tables. Code and artifact available at this https URL
subjects: Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC); Cryptography and Security (cs.CR); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
abstract: Enterprise AI agents can execute altered versions of approved actions, concurrently reuse the same permission, or retry operations whose responses were lost. These failures arise when approval and resource execution lack a shared contract. KedgeFlow specifies language-independent contracts for trusted controllers to authorize state-changing operations and privileged gateways to enforce that authority independently of agent reasoning. Inspired by OpenFlow, it connects policy checks supported by evidence, signed permission for an exact action, a shared allowance that can be consumed only once, target-side conditions for applying the change, and retained outcome records. Under trusted issuance of exact-action authority, two conditional properties establish at most one successful claim per allowance and link every governed dispatch to a matching grant, claim, and subsequent dispatch authorization, even when the agent is compromised. A reference implementation exposes this execution path to agent systems through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). In the single-resource evaluation, 6,560 concurrent ledger claim attempts yielded exactly one successful claim for each of 82 allowances. Boundary tests rejected unauthorized and altered requests before consumption. A 32-call gateway race produced one committed mock effect, and a retry after a lost response produced no additional dispatch. Deliberately permissive policy nevertheless authorized an undesirable effect, exposing the limits of execution authorization. Evaluation uses three members of the etcd coordinated key-value store on one host, synthetic authentication and authorization inputs, and a mock target that rejects stale requests. Distributed reservations, enforcement of every production access route, native crash recovery, exactly-once effects at real targets, and interoperability between independent implementations remain untested.

title: Explore This! Beat and Downbeat Tracking From a Learned Tatum Grid
comments: Accepted at the 27th International Society for Music Information Retrieval Conference (ISMIR), 2026
subjects: Sound (cs.SD); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Audio and Speech Processing (eess.AS)
abstract: State-of-the-art beat tracking is based on neural networks that model beats and downbeats as individual events, often followed by a separate Dynamic Bayesian Network (DBN) enforcing musical consistency. We propose a novel architecture that combines deep learning with differentiable theory-based modules: Specifically, we design a system that first predicts a tatum grid, then groups tatum events to beats and downbeats, explicitly modelling multiple options for the current tempo and time signature in a bar-pointer-like fashion. Our approach improves continuity metrics compared to existing DBN-free systems and is more versatile than the de-facto standard DBN, but still falls behind the best DBN-based methods on average. Given the many design choices and hyperparameters involved, we assume we have not yet explored the full potential of this idea and publish our code and invite others to explore this further.

title: Physics-informed random neural architectures on compact boundaryless multiply connected manifolds for random-operator models in machine learning and uncertainty quantification
comments: Published in Computer Methods in Applied Mechanics and Engineering}, doi:https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cma.2026.119437, 463, 119437 (2027)
abstract: We introduce stochastic physics-informed neural networks (SPINNs) for stochastic boundary-value problems (SBVPs) with random operators. The method enforces physics through a structural probabilistic coupling: a common Gaussian stochastic germ drives both the SBVP random operator and a manifold-based stochastic neural architecture. The stochastic neural network is non-feedforward and intrinsically random. A latent Gaussian field and an inhomogeneous Poisson point process on a compact, boundaryless, multiply connected manifold generate random neuron locations, geodesically local sparse connectivity, and a sparse random weight matrix, all governed by a low-dimensional hyperparameter. For deterministic inputs, the network output is random and can represent non-Gaussian random operators. Training is performed in observation space: SBVP simulations produce random observables, while the SNN defines a predictive conditional probability density function. The supervised objective combines data fidelity, through negative log-likelihood, with a cross-entropy alignment term relative to the SBVP-induced conditional distribution. The resulting target is a convex mixture of observation-induced and SBVP-induced distributions, with a dimensionless parameter controlling robustness to model--data mismatch. The shared stochastic germ yields common-random-numbers Monte Carlo estimators and reduced-variance gradients. The method uses only evaluations of the SBVP solution mapping, without differentiating or modifying it, and avoids PDE-residual or boundary-penalty losses. A stochastic elliptic problem on a periodic cylindrical surface illustrates the approach in SBVP-consistent and SBVP-misspecified regimes. A generalized-posterior formulation is also outlined for hyperparameter inference and posterior averaging without per-query reoptimization.

title: Dependency Reasoning for Aspect Sentiment Quadruple Prediction
abstract: Aspect Sentiment Quadruple Prediction (ASQP) is fundamentally a relational reasoning problem: identifying aspect-opinion-category-sentiment quadruples requires modeling structured dependencies, not merely sequential co-occurrence. Existing LLM-based approaches incorporate syntactic information indirectly, via retrieval-based demonstration selection or multi-stage training, rather than as unified, single-pass generation-time context. We present DRIFT, which linearizes dependency parse trees and injects them directly into LLM prompts as explicit relational context, enabling the model to reason over aspect-opinion dependencies rather than infer them from token proximity alone. DRIFT further integrates retrieval-augmented in-context learning and a syntax-aware LLM-based adjudication mechanism that complements exact-match evaluation under span-boundary variation. On SemEval Rest15, Rest16, and ACOS, DRIFT achieves the strongest performance among compared generative ASQP methods, reaching 54.47% and 64.10% F1 on Rest15 and Rest16, with consistent gains across short- and medium-distance aspect-opinion configurations; adjudication further shows exact-match metrics systematically underestimate semantically correct predictions.

title: FDTD Model of Noise Pollution from an AI Data Center
abstract: The sudden growth in AI data centers is raising numerous environmental concerns. Low-frequency noise pollution is a concern for local residents, that may not just be an annoyance but also carry significant health impacts. An FDTD model of sound propagation over the topography near an AI data center is presented. The topography plays a large role in the level of noise pollution, with areas of sudden elevation on either side of the river near the AI data center more susceptible to high noise levels, while areas further afield largely protected from noise pollution by the topography. Understanding the role that topography plays in noise pollution, and capturing the noise pollution in specific topographies, can help identify areas where noise mitigation strategies might be best employed.

title: Minimum Volume Optimal Transport for Multivariate Conformal Prediction
abstract: Optimal transport (OT) enables multivariate conformal prediction (CP) to construct flexible prediction sets that reflect the underlying complex distributional geometry while retaining distribution-free coverage guarantees. Existing OT-based methods typically rely on a fixed Euclidean transport cost, which can be suboptimal in terms of the volume of prediction sets. We propose Minimum-Volume OTCP, a framework that learns a Mahalanobis ground cost to directly minimize prediction-region volume over a class of positive-definite metrics. Using a metric Brenier representation, we derive a volume-based objective that depends explicitly on the Mahalanobis cost matrix and optimize it jointly with the transport map. We establish finite-sample marginal coverage of the output prediction sets and optimality of volume metrics. We further develop an individualized extension that learns covariate-dependent transport metrics, adapting the shape and orientation of prediction sets to heterogeneous conditional distributions. For this extension, we also show the asymptotic conditional coverage of our method. Simulations and real-data experiments demonstrate substantial reductions in prediction-set volume.

title: An Algebraic Approach to Constrained K-means Clustering
abstract: Clustering is typically performed using only object features, although additional information about relationships between objects may be available and can be incorporated through constraints. Among these, pairwise constraints require two objects to belong to the same cluster or to different clusters. Several extensions of the k-means algorithm accommodate such constraints, but they sometimes fail to find a feasible assignment or incur high computational cost. Motivated by these limitations, we propose an algebraic approach to k-means clustering with pairwise constraints. The algorithm simplifies the constraints using Gröbner bases before optimization, improving the efficiency of cluster assignment. It can also detect whether the constraint set has a feasible assignment before optimization. Comparative experiments with existing algorithms showed that the proposed algorithm achieved comparable or better clustering quality at a lower computational cost, particularly when the numbers of constraints and clusters were small.

title: CFG-Policy: Unified Diffusion Policy Learning Framework via Classifier-free Guidance
abstract: Diffusion policies are increasingly used in robotic control and manipulation, vision-language-action models, and world-model-based agents. Their ability to represent multimodal action distributions offers rich opportunities for exploration in reinforcement learning (RL). However, optimizing diffusion policies with RL can reduce the behavioral diversity and further limit their exploration capability. In RL post-training, directly fine-tuning a pretrained policy may also disrupt its acquired capabilities, while action-space residuals may lack the expressive power for multimodal exploration. Together, these issues reveal a common challenge across online and offline-to-online diffusion RL: improving task performance while retaining the behavioral diversity and capabilities needed for continued adaptation. We introduce CFG-Policy, a unified, plug-and-play framework that separates exploration and exploitation into two generative policies and combines their score or velocity fields during sampling through classifier-free guidance. For online RL, a frozen exploration branch sustains behavioral diversity while an exploitation branch learns from task rewards; for offline-to-online RL, a pretrained exploitation branch remains frozen while a trainable branch steers the composed behavior. CFG-Policy preserves the underlying RL objectives and improves performance with QSM and QVPO on 5 MuJoCo tasks and with Flow-SDE+PPO on 4 RoboTwin manipulation tasks. Project page is at this https URL.

title: AlphaRLM: Aligning Language Models for Literature-Grounded Symbolic Factor Discovery
subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computation and Language (cs.CL); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Portfolio Management (q-fin.PM)
abstract: Formulaic alpha mining seeks to discover executable expressions that capture predictive market signals in a vast, noisy search space. Recent LLM-based approaches use prompting, iterative search, or seed-factor evolution, leaving direct factor construction through policy learning less explored. To address this, we introduce AlphaRLM, a reinforcement-learning framework that trains LLMs to construct executable symbolic factors from financial literature without input factor expressions. AlphaRLM incorporates Literature-Guided Operator Assembly (LEGO), which conditions factor construction on literature-derived ideas and executable operators, providing semantic priors for exploration. It further aligns the generation policy with market feedback through executable-validity and grouped-return-separation rewards that capture non-monotonic structures across factor quantiles. Extensive experiments on CSI 300, CSI 1000, and S&P 500 show that AlphaRLM outperforms strong factor-mining and LLM-based baselines in annualized excess return. Notably, the 8B model achieves strong cross-market performance, highlighting the promise of literature-conditioned, market-aligned factor generation.

title: SEEK: Agentic Knowledge Graph Retrieval for Secure Code Generation
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can generate functionally correct code while introducing exploitable security weaknesses, particularly when developers specify functionality without explicit security requirements. Recent state-of-the-art approaches mitigate this problem using external security knowledge, but largely rely on flat similarity-based retrieval over independent artifacts, making it difficult to infer the relevant vulnerability space and retrieve targeted knowledge when direct matches are unavailable. We propose SEEK, an agentic Graph RAG framework for secure code generation that constructs a security knowledge graph using the Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE) taxonomy as its structural backbone and injects it with curated real-world CVE vulnerability-fix instances. At inference time, a Planner Agent predicts potential CWE weaknesses associated with the developer query, which guide Graph Scoping to restrict retrieval to relevant regions of the CWE taxonomy before deterministic multi-faceted candidate ranking. A Selection Agent subsequently validates the predicted weaknesses and retrieved candidates prior to code generation. Across five open-source LLMs, we evaluate SEEK in an out-of-distribution setting on CodeGuard+ and CyberSecEval, spanning C, C++, and Python. SEEK achieves the highest SecurePass@1 of 77.45% on CodeGuard+ and the highest aggregate ICD pass rate of 79.45% on CyberSecEval, surpassing prior approaches. Moreover, SEEK achieves 85.2% SecurePass@1 across 13 unseen CWE types with no directly linked vulnerability-fix instances, demonstrating strong generalizability, while maintaining acceptable inference latency costs.

title: DiffGA: Steering Frozen Diffusion Models for Materials Design via Evolutionary Search
abstract: Steering candidate generation toward user-defined objectives is central to inverse materials design, yet remains difficult when objectives are black-box, changing, or non-differentiable, as in many simulation- and experiment-derived properties. Generative models offer a solution but typically require retraining or fine-tuning for each new objective, demanding labeled data and substantial compute, or rely on differentiable guidance that is brittle to gradient noise and undefined for many practical targets. We present DiffGA, a retraining-free framework that injects evolutionary search into the sampling trajectory of a retrained diffusion model, evolving partially denoised states under an arbitrary black-box oracle. Because oracle evaluation often dominates campaign cost, we couple DiffGA with an on-the-fly Bayesian surrogate that reuses representations from state-of-the-art machine-learned force fields (MLFFs). A Gaussian process is fit during the campaign on the force fields's graph embeddings and, once it demonstrably ranks an unseen generation, replaces expensive property evaluations under an uncertainty-aware acquisition rule, reducing oracle cost with negligible loss of accuracy. Across three crystal-design tasks using a frozen MatterGen backbone, DiffGA outperforms diffusion-only, compute-matched, purely evolutionary, and fine-tuned baselines in oracle-assessed rates of stable, unique, and novel hits. Rather than proposing scientific compounds, we use density functional theory to quantify MLFF oracle fidelity, showing that it is a faithful proxy in key regimes but systematically biased in others, delineating when proxy-driven generative discovery can be trusted. On a representative sample, DiffGA's top hits survive first principles re-evaluation as physically realistic hits, while the surrogate-accelerated pipeline preserves this fidelity at a fraction of the cost.

title: DisCo Algebra: Why Disintegration and Combination Are Not Inverses
subjects: Probability (math.PR); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Mathematical Physics (math-ph); Category Theory (math.CT); Statistics Theory (math.ST)
abstract: We present DisCo algebra---a compositional framework for joint probability built from a symmetric cooperad (disintegration) and a symmetric operad (combination) on the bare family $\mathcal{P}_n=\mathrm{Prob}([0,1]^n)$. No probability integral transform, no external summary functions, no enrichment of objects with conditional kernels. The disintegration side uses block-wise joint CDFs as intrinsic, measure-determined 1D summaries, yielding a lossy compression. The combination side reads the same summaries and reconstructs via regular conditional measures, yielding a lossless embedding. We prove that combination followed by disintegration is the identity on admissible inputs, but disintegration followed by combination is not---the information loss is exactly the conditional KL divergence between the true conditional distribution and the conditionally independent product. This asymmetry reveals a hard limit on how much cross-block dependence can be captured by scalar block summaries.

title: What Drives AI Citations? Content, Retrieval and Model Knowledge in Generative Engine Optimization (GEO)
subjects: Information Retrieval (cs.IR); Computation and Language (cs.CL); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Social and Information Networks (cs.SI)
abstract: Generative search engines such as ChatGPT, Gemini and Perplexity now decide which Web pages users see as sources, and a growing industry of generative engine optimization advises publishers on how to earn these citations. We study what shapes citation in two 90-day collections of answers to commercial questions in contrasting markets: 158,099 answers with 468,037 citations. Comparing pages of the same website, content matters in one way: pages whose title and paragraphs match the questions people ask are cited more, whereas FAQ blocks, structured data, summary boxes and page speed appear effective only across websites. Page properties nevertheless explain little of the variation between pages of a website. Replaying the questions through the engines' APIs shows why. Every page ChatGPT cites is one its own search retrieved, and which pages that search retrieves, for sub-queries the model rewrites on every answer and that rarely coincide with Google's or Bing's results, explains far more of the variation than page properties (32% against 2.8%). Content acts mainly through this step, by matching the engine's queries in meaning. The model's own knowledge shapes it too: ChatGPT writes brands it knows into its searches, prefers websites it knows, and names brands without any supporting page, and controlled experiments show that brand names reorder its rankings of products with identical facts. Pages are thus cited when searched; brands are also named when remembered. The findings replicate in a market of small B2B vendors. We release data and code.

title: TurnCost: Turns, Not Observations: Cache-Aware Loop Engineering for Coding Agents
subjects: Software Engineering (cs.SE); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Emerging Technologies (cs.ET); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
abstract: AI coding agents operate in iterative loops: they modify code, run tools, inspect the results, and decide what to do next. We call the design of this process loop engineering, which includes context management, model selection, compaction, and termination. Existing efficiency work mainly compresses tool observations or routes selected turns to cheaper models, but the practical opportunity for these optimizations remains unclear. We analyze 600 publicly released coding-agent trajectories spanning two agent scaffolds and two language models. Median observations contain only 118-286 tokens, while the large build logs commonly used to motivate compression occur near the ninety-ninth percentile. Moreover, 98.6% of input tokens are served from a prefix cache, so flat input pricing overestimates loop cost by roughly 7x on average under near-ideal caching. We derive and empirically validate a closed-form break-even condition for model delegation. Delegation increases cost in half of the evaluated settings, near the predicted boundary. More broadly, turn count explains 84% of the variance in log trajectory cost, compared with 4% for mean observation size; the most expensive trajectories have the most turns despite having the smallest observations. These associations suggest that observation-focused methods target a secondary cost factor, and identify unnecessary turns as the larger and largely unexamined opportunity, though we do not establish that turns can be removed while holding task success fixed. We release TurnCost, a tool for re-scoring trajectory corpora under alternative caching, pricing, compression, and routing policies.

title: Energy-Guided Learning for Heat Equation with Noisy Source: Optimal Estimation and Generalization Bounds
subjects: Statistics Theory (math.ST); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Methodology (stat.ME); Machine Learning (stat.ML)
abstract: Data and the governing partial differential equations (PDEs) of continuous-time dynamical systems provide rich structure for statistical learning. A central challenge is how to integrate data with PDE constraints in a principled way to improve generalization. In this paper, we characterize the statistical estimation and generalization properties of learning solutions to the heat equation with a noisy source function from finite, randomly sampled data. We first derive a novel variational formulation, which we characterize as the minimizer of loss function for an energy regularized and ellipticity debiased Sobolev regression. By formulating the learning task as a supervised problem over space-time domains under physically meaningful norms, our approach goes beyond the traditional supervised learning framework by effectively leveraging \emph{auxiliary data}---samples of the source function of the heat equation---to design a \emph{physics-informed energy regularization}. Our analysis reveals that learning in linear parabolic PDEs exhibits intrinsic anisotropy between spatial and temporal regularity, in sharp contrast to the static elliptic problems, leading to fundamentally different estimation and generalization behaviors. Specifically, we derive non-asymptotically rate-optimal estimation errors, as well as generalization error, which explicitly capture the interplay among temporal sampling, spatial resolution, and solution smoothness. Our numerical experiments demonstrate substantial orders of magnitude of reduction in testing errors against various physics-informed neural network methods on various parabolic and hyperbolic PDEs.

title: Data-Topology Compatibility Enables Personalization in Decentralized Learning
abstract: Decentralized learning must balance collaboration with personalization across heterogeneous agents. This paper studies when cooperation can support statistically coherent groups of personalized models. We show that data-topology compatibility enables robust orbit-wise personalization: when local objectives and communication topology have (approximately) compatible automorphisms, agents within an orbit share (approximately) equal limiting distributions, while different orbits remain distinct without explicit personalization. This creates a new intermediate regime between global consensus and independent local learning. Under exact data-topology compatibility, as a reference system, we decompose the stochastic learning dynamics into orbit-level and transverse components, derive a necessary and sufficient stability criterion for distributional synchronization, and characterize the orbit-structured stationary law. Modelling an approximate data-topology compatible system as an $\varepsilon$-perturbed reference system, we prove the introduced errors have uniform-in-time and stationary $O(\varepsilon)$ bounds in 2-Wasserstein distance. We also prove sufficient conditions for lower stationary average excess risk than both independent local training and the best single shared parameter. Experiments on synthetic data, MNIST, and CIFAR-10 are in full agreement with the theory. The code is available at this https URL.

title: Sanzaru: Benchmarking Protocol Formation under Epistemic & Communication Asymmetry
abstract: A language model's ability to solve a task individually does not ensure that a team can solve it under unequal access to information and communication. SANZARU examines this gap through cooperative bomb-defusal puzzles adapted from BOMBANANA! (Lefto Studio, 2026). Task information and action authority are divided among three agents: one cannot hear, another cannot speak, and the third cannot see. The benchmark contains 120 puzzle instances across seven families, each targeting a distinct coordination ability. Across 1512 episodes, 7 models achieve an overall success rate of 49%, ranging from 20% to 86% under the evaluated configurations. Teams develop or adopt diverse communication protocols, from simple gesture codes to Morse and encodings of entire manuals. Yet trace analysis attributes about 60% of 771 team losses to communication, and agents attempt to use channels unavailable to their teammates despite explicit role instructions. Together, task outcomes and interaction traces enable evaluation of both collaborative performance and perspective taking throughout cooperation. The benchmark is available at this https URL.

title: Physics Foundation Models for Efficient Control of Fluid Flows
abstract: We investigate whether a physics foundation model (PFM) pretrained for PDE forecasting can be repurposed for closed-loop fluid-flow control. We construct a PFM-based controller by attaching lightweight Gaussian actor and critic heads to frozen pretrained representations and train the policy using proximal policy optimization (PPO). We evaluate the approach on HydroGym's two-dimensional Kolmogorov-flow environment using vorticity observations at \(64\times64\) and \(128\times128\) resolutions and Reynolds numbers \(\mathrm{Re}=100\) and \(200\). Across these settings, we compare the frozen PFM controller against a baseline MLP policy trained with the same PPO framework. The PFM controller achieves consistently higher reward while requiring smaller executed action magnitudes over training, indicating improved control performance with reduced control effort. These results provide initial evidence that representations learned through self-supervised next-frame prediction can be transferred directly to closed-loop fluid flow control. Project page: this https URL.

title: SAFE-KV: Causal Suffix Repair for Behavior-Preserving Non-Prefix KV Cache Reuse in RAG
comments: Accepted to Findings of AACL-IJCNLP 2026. 36 pages, 5 figures, 33 tables. Code: this https URL
abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) reuses the same documents across many requests, making non-prefix KV-cache reuse attractive. Yet a cached document state is not reusable text: it is a context-conditioned causal state whose keys and values depend on the prefix, position, and preceding documents under which it was computed. We formulate non-prefix KV reuse as a behavior-preservation problem with full prefill on the exact prompt as the reference, and introduce SAFE-KV, which repairs a composed cache by re-encoding the causal suffix from a selected start document. On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, prefix-conditioned composition preserves only 47.2% of HotpotQA-500 and 37.8% of 2Wiki-500 full-prefill answers; SAFE-KV with risk-guided K2 selection restores 99.8%/98.4% (donor-copy protocol) and 100.0%/98.4% with actual suffix forwarding. Document-only and fixed-window repairs recover far less, because the document states after the repaired region keep histories that omit it. Reuse without repair is exact up to four documents and degrades at sixteen, where suffix repair recovers 98-100%. Faithful repair re-encodes most of the context, so in a single-request L40S study SAFE-KV's operating rule serves every workload by full prefill. SAFE-KV thus establishes the causal-state contract for non-prefix reuse and a validated repair mechanism that meets it.

title: MoSAIC: Learning DAG Scheduling Heuristics from Optimal Schedules through Motif-Aware Recovery and LLM-Guided Reasoning
subjects: Hardware Architecture (cs.AR); Information Retrieval (cs.IR); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
abstract: Efficient task scheduling in heterogeneous computing systems remains a fundamental challenge in embedded and high-level synthesis flows. This paper presents MoSAIC (Motif-aware Scheduling with AI-driven Cognition), a learning-based framework that bridges the gap between exact and heuristic scheduling approaches for DAG-based applications. The system uses the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs) to learn the relationships between DAG structures and scheduling priority functions. The framework first leverages the OR-Tools CP-SAT solver [4] to generate optimal schedules, which are then used to supervise the learning of compact priority-based scheduling functions through Bayesian Optimization. These learned heuristics capture relationships between scheduling decisions and structural graph features such as rank, depth, and fanout, enabling the construction of a reusable knowledge base across diverse DAG instances. Experimental results across synthetic graph families and real-world benchmarks, including PolyBench and MachSuite, show that the learned heuristics consistently improve over classical approaches such as HEFT [2], while maintaining low runtime overhead. The results indicate that combining optimal supervision with learning-based generalization provides a practical approach for scalable and adaptive task scheduling.

title: Non-Euclidean Gradient Descent Has Many Edges of Stability
abstract: Recent observations that deep learning models train at the edge of stability have renewed interest in understanding stability properties of classical optimization algorithms. For quadratic objectives, standard gradient descent has a sharp stability threshold: it converges from every initialization when $\eta<2/L$, diverges from almost every initialization when $\eta>2/L$, and diverges from every nonzero initialization when $\eta>2/\mu$. For non-Euclidean gradient descent, the corresponding known guarantees are weaker: convergence holds for every initialization when $\eta<2/S$, where $S$ is the generalized sharpness, while every nonzero initialization diverges when $\eta>2/\mu$. The behavior in the intermediate regime $2/S<\eta<2/\mu$ is not fully characterized. We show that Hilbertian norms are the only ones for which $2/S$ is an almost-everywhere sharp threshold for every positive-definite quadratic objective. Using linear conjugacy between non-Euclidean and Euclidean gradient descent, we show that for general norms the intermediate regime can contain arbitrarily many edges of stability associated with distinct attracting directions. We identify a forward-invariant region of exponentially divergent directions beyond the generalized stability threshold. When the directions of minimum curvature are finite and nondegenerate, we prove that, sufficiently close to $2/\mu$ from below, only their invariant directions remain convergent. We give smooth two-dimensional constructions with arbitrarily many distinct thresholds, arbitrarily large relative threshold separation and show these properties to be stable.

title: Explicit Bounds on Hoffman Constants for Sparse Polyhedral Regularizers
subjects: Optimization and Control (math.OC); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Statistics Theory (math.ST)
abstract: Hoffman constants quantify the distance to the solution set of a polyhedral system in terms of its residual; they control error bounds, geometric conditioning, the convergence rate of first-order iterative algorithms, and the stability of regression estimators to target perturbations. Despite their importance, explicit values of Hoffman constants are rarely available due to their computational complexity. In this paper, we derive explicit bounds on the Hoffman constant for a class of structured polyhedral systems arising in sparse regularization. We show that the constants admit a decomposition into spectral, geometric, and interaction components, which together determine their scaling behavior. This framework explains the gap between worst-case dimension-dependent bounds and the favorable conditioning observed empirically in structured problems. As a primary application, we analyze $\ell_1$-regularized least squares, demonstrating that the effective constants depend on low-dimensional active subspaces rather than the ambient dimension. We then extend to the elastic net and adaptive $\ell_1$-regularized formulations, demonstrating how the underlying optimization geometry is altered by the $\ell_2$ penalty and reweighting scheme. Furthermore, we relate our results to classical statistical assumptions and show that the restricted eigenvalue condition bounds only the primal curvature of the active set, leaving the dual interaction geometry unconstrained and is thus insufficient alone for fast theoretical convergence rates. We further show standard $\ell_\infty$ coherence conditions do not yield dimension-independent Euclidean bounds to close this gap. Our theoretical results show that Hoffman constants admit explicit, interpretable forms in structured regression settings and, in practice, provide actionable tools for post-hoc feature pruning and a priori optimal hyperparameter selection.

title: What a Data Release Must Preserve for Off-Policy Evaluation
abstract: In off-policy evaluation, merging decision-time histories that matter differently for a specified policy value or comparison can make that evaluation unidentified, even with observed actions and outcomes and known behavior and target policies. We characterize which distinctions must be preserved: identification holds if and only if the action-specific evaluation weights are constant within each released record, and the coarsest exact release groups histories by these weights. For normalized outcomes, the largest sharp width induced by the release equals a behavior-weighted within-record radius of these weights. The same radius becomes a release-design objective when each record may be refined into at most $m$ categories. The optimum has an exact $m$-center characterization. When behavior does not vary within a released record, we give a finite-data repair algorithm whose maximum evaluation-weight radius is at most twice the finite-data optimum. For a fixed action-outcome distribution within a released record, a distinct sharp-identification problem remains. Under the same condition, the action-specific outcome distributions are identified, and optimizing over their couplings gives the sharp interval. We construct an AIPW envelope containing this sharp interval; it matches the interval for all such outcome distributions exactly when the extreme within-record action-coefficient vectors take at most two values in each action coordinate. In 24 KuaiRec tasks, the repair algorithm yields a 93% median reduction in mean pairwise sharp width at $m=64$ relative to the unrepaired release.

title: SuperAI: Merging Capabilities Across Heterogeneous Foundation Models
abstract: Enabling the reuse and composition of knowledge and capabilities distributed across foundation models is an important step toward building scalable artificial intelligence (AI) systems. However, architectural differences and incompatible representations make it difficult to transfer and integrate these capabilities through a unified cross-model interface. To address this challenge, we propose SuperAI, a cross-architecture multi-model fusion framework that integrates complementary capabilities from multiple source models into a host model through orthogonal alignment of low-dimensional task-relevant representations. Specifically, we first extract task-relevant representations from the source models and the host model using shared anchor samples, and apply principal component analysis (PCA) to construct low-dimensional functional subspaces with the same dimensionality. Next, we use orthogonal Procrustes mappings to align the source and host coordinate systems, establishing cross-model correspondences while preserving the internal geometry of each source subspace. Finally, we train a lightweight residual multilayer perceptron (MLP) with joint supervision on task outputs and source-model increments, learning input-dependent residual increments that are injected into the host model for multi-model capability fusion. Experiments on three host models across 15 capability domains show that SuperAI achieves higher average domain scores than the evaluated cross-architecture fusion methods and better preserves general capabilities as the number of source models increases. Ablation studies further support the effectiveness of orthogonal alignment, nonlinear residual mapping, and joint supervision.

title: Deep Neural Mixed Models for Nonlinear Longitudinal Prediction with Subject-Specific Heterogeneity
abstract: Longitudinal health data often exhibit within-subject correlation, subject-specific heterogeneity, and complex nonlinear predictor--response relationships that may not be adequately captured by conventional mixed models. We propose a Deep Generalized Neural Network Mixed Model (DGNMM) that extends the GLMM framework by using a deep neural network to learn nonlinear population-level relationships while incorporating directly trainable, regularized subject-specific effects to capture individual heterogeneity. The model is estimated using prediction-oriented stochastic optimization with separate regularization of the neural-network parameters and subject-specific effects. This formulation allows us to investigate when increased nonlinear representation capacity provides additional predictive benefit in the presence of subject-specific heterogeneity. A simulation study varies population-level nonlinearity and subject-specific heterogeneity and compares DGNMM with GLMM, artificial neural network (ANN), Maity--Pal (MP), and GNMM alternatives for continuous and binary longitudinal outcomes. In the real-data application, DGNMM achieved the lowest MSPE for continuous depression and anxiety prediction, while alternative models remained competitive for binary outcomes. Exploratory subject-level analyses showed heterogeneous predictive gains across individuals, but the magnitude of the estimated subject-specific effects was not significantly associated with predictive gain. Overall, increased nonlinear representation capacity was most beneficial for continuous prediction under nonlinear response structures, while greater subject-specific heterogeneity did not systematically yield larger predictive gains.

title: CoLA: Multi-VLA Coordination via Learned Adapters
comments: 22 pages, 5 figures. Equal contribution: Ahaskar Kashyap, Jiawen Zong, Boyu Ma. Code: this https URL
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are typically deployed as isolated single-agent policies. When several such agents share a workspace, they can coordinate implicitly, by observing one another, or explicitly, by exchanging messages, but it remains unclear when explicit communication becomes necessary. We introduce CoLA (Coordination via Learned Adapters), which keeps each agent's VLA backbone frozen and trains a lightweight message channel and a per-arm diffusion action head on top, with fully decentralised execution. Across three tasks that differ in how much each agent can observe, the channel matters only when information is private. On an occluded tray handover, where the box's colour marker is visible to one agent only, CoLA reaches 76.0% success versus 1.3% with messages zeroed throughout training. On two-arm and three-arm handover tasks, removing messages has no measurable effect with a shared overhead camera (90.6% vs. 88.3% at two arms; 63.5% vs. 60.0% at three), but lowers success on the two-arm task's wrist-only variant (74.8% vs. 64.3%). This architecture generalises across different VLA backbones as well. With a frozen $\pi_{0.5}$ backbone on the same occluded tray task, CoLA matches the overall success rate of a LoRA-fine-tuned baseline (37.3% vs. 34.7%) using a fraction of the trainable parameters. When CoLA places the box, it selects the correct tray 71.8% of the time, whereas the independently fine-tuned baseline, whose placing arm never sees the marker, selects it at chance level (34.7% against 33.3%).

title: JSIR: An Audio-Aligned, Multi-Task Dataset of Jazz Standard Recordings
comments: Submitted to IEEE ICASSP 2027; 5 pages, 1 figure
subjects: Sound (cs.SD); Digital Libraries (cs.DL); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Multimedia (cs.MM); Audio and Speech Processing (eess.AS)
abstract: Beat tracking, chord estimation, and structure analysis are staple tasks of music information retrieval. Their datasets are drawn largely from Western popular music, and jazz remains a repertoire on which state-of-the-art systems underperform. We present JSIR, the Jazz Standards dataset for Information Retrieval. Its 267 recordings of 44 jazz standards span 25.6 hours, 3.7 times the audio of JAAH, the closest existing resource. For each recording, we provide annotations for beat and downbeat positions, chords, and sections, all produced by a jazz musician and revised in several passes. In baseline experiments, models trained with JSIR also improve on other jazz datasets: the downbeat F-measure of a state-of-the-art beat tracker rises from 87.7% to 89.2%, and the seventh-chord accuracy of a pop-trained chord estimator on JAAH from 34% to 41%. We publicly release the annotations, the annotation tool used to create them, and a web application that displays them in sync with the audio.

title: LiveAnon: Improving Privacy and Utility in Streaming Speaker Anonymization with Codec Language Models
subjects: Audio and Speech Processing (eess.AS); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Sound (cs.SD)
abstract: Speaker anonymization (SA) aims to conceal speaker identity while preserving linguistic content and emotion, but existing streaming systems often lose emotion information through discrete content bottlenecks or require emotion-specific modeling. We present LiveAnon, a voice-conversion-based streaming SA system that directly conditions an autoregressive codec language model on hidden features from a pretrained streaming ASR encoder, preserving emotion without emotion-specific supervision. To reduce codec-generation latency, we introduce capped RVQ decoding, which preserves dependencies among coarse codebooks while predicting the remaining codebooks in parallel. Under VPC24, LiveAnon improves intelligibility and emotion preservation over fixed-target Stream-Voice-Anon (SVA), a strong prior streaming SA system, matches emotion-prompted SVA in emotion preservation, and achieves the strongest semi-informed privacy among streaming systems. Under VPC26, it ranks second across all metrics among the evaluated anonymization systems, demonstrating a strong privacy-utility balance.

title: Sensitivity or Criterion? Measuring and Moving When Language Models Act
subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
abstract: Before an agent acts, it must decide whether action is warranted. A single accuracy cannot distinguish failure to recognize a warranted action from reluctance to act. Signal-detection theory separates sensitivity from criterion, but criteria estimated from authored binary labels depend on each benchmark's example mix. We introduce FlipAct, a diagnostic of tool use in physical states. A rule over annotated tool properties computes each answer and a graded evidence score, fixing the Yes/No boundary at zero across models. Questions form 2-by-2 quads that hold required knowledge fixed while the state flips. The slope of the fitted Yes-rate curve measures sensitivity; its crossing at one half measures criterion. Across 44 open models, sensitivity rises with size within a family, and its ranking agrees with three of four external when-to-act benchmarks. Models respond to evidence sign rather than magnitude, accepting actions that leave the state no better about as often as helpful ones. When Yes means act, most models are conservative across rephrasings; in some, this partly reflects a preference for No. Criterion is not determined by size. Activation steering shifts criterion with weights fixed; distillation from a model's own steered copy puts the shift into its weights without a significant sensitivity change. The distilled shift transfers to six external benchmarks, including two without Yes/No answers, while criterion-free AUC is preserved on the five benchmarks where it is available. Accuracy improves where models start conservative and declines or remains within error where they start permissive. Project page: this https URL

title: BridgeCodec: Mamba Enhanced Neural Audio Codec with Schrödinger Bridge at Low Bitrate
subjects: Sound (cs.SD); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Audio and Speech Processing (eess.AS)
abstract: Neural audio codecs achieve remarkable performance but operate as closed ecosystems with rigidly co-trained encoderdecoder pairs, severely hindering interoperability. To resolve this, we propose BridgeCodec, a versatile framework that decouples these pairs by translating latent representations between mismatched, frozen endpoints. We formulate this cross-codec translation as a Schrödinger Bridge optimal transport problem, enabling robust mapping between disparate distributions without predefined noise priors. To efficiently capture longrange speech temporal dependencies, we integrate a Mambaenhanced U-Net architecture. We validate BridgeCodec on an extreme deployment scenario: mapping a lightweight 8 kHz source encoder directly to a 48 kHz target decoder at an ultralow bitrate of 1 kbps. Experimental results demonstrate that BridgeCodec achieves superior wideband reconstruction and high perceptual quality, successfully bridging heavily bottlenecked, heterogeneous codecs.

title: Personalized Physiological-Model-Based Neural Network for Glucose Forecasting in Type 1 Diabetes
abstract: Accurate, physiologically consistent glucose forecasts could help people with type 1 diabetes respond to impending excursions. We applied our physiological-model-based neural network (PMB--NN) framework to glucose forecasting. A temporal convolutional network (TCN) used 180 min of history, constrained during training by a personalized four-parameter physiological model. The main PMB--NN combined forecast and neural--physiological agreement losses; a three-term variant additionally fitted physiological predictions to measured glucose. Data comprised 6--8 weeks of continuous glucose monitoring, pump, and meal records from 25 AZT1D participants. Person-specific models used chronological 70/10/20 train/validation/test splits and 30-, 60-, and 120-min horizons. Median mean absolute errors were 16.24, 25.00, and 30.20 mg/dL with basal insulin records and 15.38, 24.21, and 31.79 mg/dL before these records became available. In the latter setting, PMB--NN had the lowest median error at 30 and 60 min; it outperformed the physiological model alone in all six settings. In input-increase tests, glucose predictions changed in the expected direction for 85\% of correction boluses and 100\% of carbohydrate rescues, versus 57\% for active insulin and 56\% for active carbohydrates. Most standalone physiological fits showed locally distinguishable parameter effects, with glucose-related coefficients more stable under resampling than insulin- or carbohydrate-related coefficients. The three-term variant improved hyperglycaemia accuracy with basal records, but did not significantly change overall MAE and reduced directional plausibility in three tests. PMB--NN combines personalized forecasting with an explicit physiological model, allowing assessment of predictive accuracy, physiological response behavior, and participant-specific coefficients.

title: AlphaPilot: Multi-Turn Tool-Using LLM Agents for Adaptive Alpha Mining with Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Formulaic alpha mining seeks interpretable expressions that rank assets by future returns. The task is challenging because it demands simultaneous processing of unstructured market descriptions, historical data, and quantitative evaluation of candidate factors, yet most existing methods exploit only a subset of these signals. We introduce AlphaPilot, a reinforcement-learning framework that trains multi-turn tool-using LLM agents for adaptive alpha mining. The agent conditions on market descriptions, proposes factor expressions, queries real-data evaluator feedback, and updates a retained factor pool across turns. This design jointly leverages market text, LLM financial knowledge, real data, and evaluation feedback. At inference time, AlphaPilot performs day-by-day search and pool updates to adapt to shifting market regimes. Across three independent runs in out-of-sample rolling backtests on CSI300 and CSI500, AlphaPilot achieves mean total returns of 42.93% and 54.19%, with mean Sharpe ratios of 2.46 and 2.86, respectively. It attains the highest mean total return, Sharpe, and RankIC among the evaluated methods on both universes.

title: RF Fingerprinting of DSP Implementations using Machine Learning: An Over-the-Air Case Study
abstract: Radio frequency fingerprinting aims to identify transmitters by exploiting small differences in the emitted signal waveform. Common approaches exploit hardware-dependent imperfections for that purpose. This work instead investigates whether differences between digital signal processing implementations of a transmitter can be identified from their radiated signals. As a practical case study, five different software-based DSP implementations for generating a 2-FSK RTTY communication waveform are considered. In a monitoring receiver, a classifier can identify these DSP implementations using convolutional neural networks that are trained on augmented software-generated signals represented as raw IQ, power spectrum or instantaneous frequency. The trained networks are evaluated on over-the-air recordings obtained using a shortwave transceiver and a software-defined radio receiver. The best neural network combines IQ and the power spectrum representation and achieves an accuracy of up to 90%. The study further examines the influence of the signal SNR and the observation bandwidth on the classification accuracy. The results demonstrate that DSP implementations leave distinguishable characteristics in the transmitted signals and suggest that DSP-dependent fingerprinting can provide complementary information for specific emitter identification systems.

title: Poisoned into Action: Context Attacks on Typed Decision Workflows
comments: 13 pages, 3 figures. Code available at this https URL
abstract: Typed decision interfaces restrict models to predefined actions, yet schema-valid choices can still trigger policy-violating state changes. Evaluating context poisoning thus requires connecting model decisions to execution outcomes while accounting for legitimate automation retained by defenses. We introduce an execution-aware protocol tracing poisoned evidence through retrieval, model choice, automated action, and persisted state. We evaluate it with 1,659 fresh calls to Jev-1.13.0 across 20 development tasks in two synthetic workflows, using three repetitions per condition. Under natural retrieval, a standalone payload reaches all 60 trials and produces five security-violating executions, while a carrier-payload pair exposes the payload in 57 trials and produces one violation. An initial source-exclusion gate blocks the pair's observed violation but also withholds ten otherwise correct attacked decisions and sixteen correct clean decisions. Correcting its empty-scope behavior restores twelve clean decisions without additional model calls. Factorial controls show that adding correct evidence reduces wrong executions from 119/120 to 55/120 in the semantic arm and from 60/120 to zero in the neutral arm, suggesting that much of the improvement reflects general evidence value rather than attack-specific protection. Three prespecified contrasts are not statistically supported after Holm correction, so the findings remain exploratory. The protocol provides an auditable framework for studying which poisoning-induced errors reach execution and how much correct automation defenses preserve. Code is available at this https URL.

title: Beyond Aggregate Drift: Optimal Client-Specific Windows in Federated Learning
abstract: We study federated learning from continuously arriving data: each client samples from its own distribution, these distributions drift over time, and the server must track the minimizer of the clients' weighted average loss. Clients are not alike as they collect data at different rates, with different noise, and change at different speeds. The main question is how much history should each one keep? A single shared window must serve every client at once, and so makes a fast-changing client carry the sampling noise of a slow, nearly stationary one. We give each client a memory of its own, sized to that client's noise, arrival rate, and drift, and refresh it by restarted accelerated method that starts from a common point. The tracking error is then bounded by \[ R\left(\sum_m w_m^{3/2}\,\sigma_m\sqrt{\gamma_m/\lambda_m}\right)^{2/3}, \] for clients with weight $w_m$, noise $\sigma_m$, arrival rate $\lambda_m$, and drift rate $\gamma_m$ on a domain of diameter $R$. This is never worse than what any common window can achieve, and strictly better whenever noise and drift are spread unevenly across clients. A lower bound that puts different groups of clients on different drift clocks shows this quantity is the right one. The two bounds agree up to a constant whenever the clients occupy boundedly many refresh scales, and in general differ only by the sixth root of the number of scales. Experiments show the gain comes from the memory rather than from the solver: it persists across accelerated, stochastic-gradient, and one-step methods, and against a separately tuned common-memory baseline.

title: Vision-Predictor-Action: Towards Efficient Embodied AI via Neuro-Symbolic JEPA Predictors
comments: 26 pages, 5 figures, 4 tables. Code: this https URL | Checkpoints: this https URL | Zenodo: this https URL
subjects: Logic in Computer Science (cs.LO); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models commonly generate robot actions token by token through Large Language Model (LLM) decoders, causing inference latency to grow with action sequence length and limiting closed-loop control frequency. We present Goal-Conditioned Vision-Predictor-Action (VPA), which replaces autoregressive decoders with a lightweight latent control loop. A shared vision encoder and a frozen text encoder embed observations, goal images, and instructions; a neuro-symbolic selector chooses a discrete skill; a Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) predictor forecasts the next latent state; and a flow-matching solver generates an entire action chunk in a few integration steps, so that sequential network evaluations per decision step do not depend on the action horizon. We analyze inference complexity, regularization against representation collapse, and conditions under which latent sub-goal thresholding limits error accumulation across task phases. As an initial proof of concept, we evaluated VPA on the LIBERO-10 suite. The trainable model has under 20M parameters (checkpoint under 75 MB, excluding a frozen 63.4M-parameter CLIP text encoder); a decision step of a single-camera reference configuration takes 10-14 ms on an Apple M4; and trained only on LIBERO-10 demonstrations in under three hours on a single GPU, a two-camera policy succeeded in 40.0% of 200 evaluation episodes. These preliminary results from a single training run suggest the approach is workable. Code and weights are available at this https URL and this https URL, and archived at this https URL.

title: Latent-Space Importance Weighting under Covariate Shift
abstract: In this work, we propose a transfer learning algorithm for covariate shift, integrating sample reweighting with representation learning. A key feature of our approach is the use of a lower-dimensional latent space for modeling, in contrast to conventional methods that operate directly in the high-dimensional ambient space. Our method estimates the density ratio of learned latent features for downstream weighted prediction. We establish explicit target-domain excess-risk rates with independent data folds for strictly sufficient learned representations with regular learned-space prediction scores and density ratios. We give dimension comparisons under stated smoothness conditions and a variance comparison for true weights and a fixed predictor. General finite-sample inequalities retain representation-quality errors. Experiments on simulated and real-world datasets demonstrate gains from combining learned representations and latent weighting, and reveal sensitivity to initialization and domain choice.

title: Joint Contrastive-Adversarial Representation Learning for Unsupervised Domain Adaptation
abstract: Effective unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) requires a representation that captures transferable structure from both the labeled source domain and the unlabeled target domain. We introduce Joint Contrastive-Adversarial Representation Learning (JCAR), a two-stage framework that learns a common representation from the union of unlabeled source and target samples by combining contrastive learning with adversarial domain alignment, and then freezes the representation to fit a source-supervised predictor. We establish a non-asymptotic excess-risk bound for this procedure that couples representation and domain-discriminator estimation while separating downstream prediction, with explicit neural-network approximation errors. Under the stated assumptions and common Hölder smoothness $\beta\geq1$, the bound identifies a sufficiently large unlabeled-sample regime in which the downstream rate is $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(m^{-\beta/(2\beta+d)})$, where $m$ counts labeled source samples and logarithmic factors are suppressed. The labeled-sample exponent is governed by the latent dimension $d$ rather than the ambient dimension $p$, which enters the pretraining cost. Experiments on Office-31, Office-Home, and DomainNet demonstrate clear transfer gains across diverse domain shifts, with particularly strong performance when representations are learned from scratch.

title: Screening Collapse under Recursive Synthetic Data
abstract: Recursive synthetic-data training can degrade a fitted model, but its effects on the variable-screening stage that precedes model fitting are less understood. When each generation labels data for the next, a marginal screener ranks variables against the current pseudo-label target rather than the original response. Across generations, this target drift can erode or reverse the active--inactive score margin and cause screening to discard variables that clean-label screening would retain. We call this process \emph{screening collapse}. In a Gaussian linear model with minimum-norm recursive generators, we establish finite-sample screening bounds, characterize a late-generation information-loss limit, and derive a minimax impossibility result. Screening collapse can precede and compound ordinary model collapse: omitted variables incur a covariance-weighted loss that no refit restricted to the selected variables can eliminate, while recursive labels further degrade estimation on the retained variables. We also examine two approaches to mitigating screening collapse. Fixed-fraction real-label retention preserves a clean-label component but leaves resolution fixed, whereas data accumulation can avoid screening collapse if the pooled target preserves a positive margin and the growing sample resolves it. Numerical experiments on gene-expression data support the theoretical findings.

title: ProtoPur: Prototype-Purity Pseudo-Labeling for Weakly Supervised Instance Learning in Pathology
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
abstract: Weak bag-level labels are widely available in computational pathology, whereas reliable instance-level annotations for whole-slide images remain expensive and ambiguous. Weakly supervised multiple instance learning (MIL) achieves strong bag-level classification, but instance-level supervision from attention scores, model predictions, negative bags, or spatial refinement may fail to identify class-specific local evidence. We propose ProtoPur, a prototype-purity pseudo-labeling method for weakly supervised instance-level learning in pathology whole-slide images. ProtoPur estimates class-balanced local purity over prototype regions constructed from frozen foundation-model features, and assigns pseudo-labels to high-purity regions strongly associated with a target class. This purity-first design separates class-specific evidence from negative or shared morphology, with coverage used only to ensure sufficient pseudo-label assignment. We provide a PAC-style analysis showing that the risk of an instance classifier trained with ProtoPur pseudo-labels can be decomposed into a standard uniform-convergence term and a ProtoPur-specific pseudo-label noise term, comprising selected-region mismatch and a coverage residual. Experiments on three public whole-slide image datasets with two pathology foundation encoders show that ProtoPur consistently improves instance-level performance across multiple MIL backbones while maintaining competitive bag-level performance. Pseudo-label quality comparisons on two public datasets further demonstrate that prototype-purity selection provides stronger instance supervision. These results suggest that the foundation-model features contain exploitable instance-level supervision signals, and ProtoPur is a way to reveal and use these signals from weak bag labels without requiring dense instance annotations.

title: When do explicit penalties improve flow matching?
subjects: Machine Learning (stat.ML); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Statistics Theory (math.ST)
abstract: Flow matching can learn structure directly from data, raising the question of when additional constraints improve generation. We study penalties that encode such constraints, with physics-informed flow matching as a motivating example. Satisfying a constraint more closely need not make the generated distribution more accurate. We therefore compare penalised and unpenalised generative modelling through their expected squared $2$-Wasserstein error. Our analysis covers both vector-valued and functional data in a Hilbert-space setting. We first derive geometric criteria that account for constraint violations and the distribution of samples after projection onto the constraint set. We then solve the statistical comparison explicitly for specific velocity-field classes and constraints via flow matching. In this model, penalisation improves accuracy exactly when the reduction in estimation variance outweighs the increase in squared bias. The resulting formula shows how this trade-off depends on sample size, the model class, the noise schedule, and the penalty weight.

title: Notes on Uniform Policy Score Bounds and Lipschitz Continuity for Truncated Gaussian, Product Cauchy, Boltzmann, and Softmax Policies
abstract: We establish uniform score bounds and Lipschitz continuity for truncated Gaussian, Cauchy, Boltzmann, and softmax policies under explicitly stated parameterizations.

title: Adaptive Robust Confidence Sets in High Dimensions
subjects: Statistics Theory (math.ST); Data Structures and Algorithms (cs.DS); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Methodology (stat.ME); Machine Learning (stat.ML)
abstract: We study adaptive confidence sets for mean vectors of multivariate Gaussians with identity covariance under Huber contamination when the contamination proportion is unknown. We show that an information-theoretically optimal adaptive confidence set can be constructed by simultaneously quantifying uncertainty across all one-dimensional projections. The resulting confidence set achieves the optimal diameter and reveals a substantial adaptation cost compared with the minimax estimation error. Although statistically optimal, this construction is computationally infeasible. We establish a Statistical Query (SQ) lower bound showing that achieving diameter $O(m^{-1/2})$ requires either exponentially many queries or query tolerance $d^{-\Omega(m)}$. Thus, in contrast to robust mean estimation, adaptation to the unknown contamination proportion incurs both a statistical cost and a computational barrier within the SQ framework. Finally, we give a low-degree moment-matching algorithm that constructs an adaptive confidence set using $d^{O(m)}$ samples and time. Its diameter bound contains an additional $O(m^{-1/2})$ term beyond the information-theoretic rate, matching the dependence on $m$ in the SQ lower bound. Together, these results characterize the statistical limits of adaptive robust confidence sets under Huber contamination and quantify a computational barrier within the SQ framework.

title: Enhancing Zero-Shot Domain Transfer in Low-Resource Sentiment Analysis: A Case Study in Marathi
abstract: Sentiment analysis is a key task in Natural Language Processing that determines the polarity of opinions in text. For low-resource languages like Marathi--where limited data prevents the direct use of standard statistical methods--models are often trained on single-domain datasets. While this yields strong in-domain performance, it leads to poor generalization to unseen domains. Recent studies highlight the need for domain-robust systems that can handle diverse real-world content through multi-domain modeling. This study investigates how multi-domain training improves sentiment classification for unseen Marathi domains. Models are trained using single-domain, two-domain, and three-domain dataset combinations. Results show that two-domain training improves accuracy on unseen domains by about 8\% compared to single-domain training.
